docs.title: 第 10 章 · 微分形式的积分
docs.text: 状态：已展开。Stokes 定理给陈述与证明思路；完整证明需第 9 章反函数/隐函数工具。 所属：Rudin 体系 · 第 10 章 · 微分形式的积分 出处：Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis，第 10 章。

docs.title: 前置
docs.text:
• 线性代数、行列式；
  • 第 9 章：多元微分、反函数定理；
  • 第 6 章：积分。

docs.title: 10.1 微分形式
docs.text:
设 \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) 开。一个 \(k\)-形式可写成

\[ \omega=\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n} f_{i_1\cdots i_k}(x)\,dx_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_{i_k}, \]

其中 \(f_I\) 是光滑函数，\(\wedge\) 是反称双线性积：

\[ dx_i\wedge dx_j=-dx_j\wedge dx_i,\qquad dx_i\wedge dx_i=0. \]

外微分：

\[ d\omega=\sum_I df_I\wedge dx_I =\sum_I\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{\partial f_I}{\partial x_j}dx_j\wedge dx_I. \]

docs.title: 定理 10.1（d² = 0）
docs.text:
对光滑形式 \(\omega\)，有

\[ d(d\omega)=0. \]

证明：由

\[ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j} =\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_j\partial x_i} \]

与 \(dx_i\wedge dx_j=-dx_j\wedge dx_i\)，混合偏导项两两抵消。证毕。

闭形式：\(d\omega=0\)。恰当形式：\(\omega=d\eta\)。定理 10.1 说明恰当 ⇒ 闭；反之一般不对，取决于区域拓扑。

docs.title: 10.2 单纯形与链
docs.text:
标准 \(k\)-单纯形：

\[ \Delta^k=\left\{(t_1,\dots,t_k):t_i\ge0,\ \sum t_i\le1\right\}. \]

奇异 \(k\)-单纯形是光滑映射 \(\sigma:\Delta^k\to U\)。\(k\)-链是有限形式和 \(\sum a_i\sigma_i\)。

边界：

\[ \partial\sigma=\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^i\sigma\circ F_i, \]

其中 \(F_i\) 是把标准单纯形的第 \(i\) 个面嵌入的仿射映射。

docs.title: 定理 10.2（∂² = 0）
docs.text:
\[ \partial(\partial\sigma)=0. \]

证明：按面映射的组合逐项计算，符号 \((-1)^{i+j}\) 在两次面映射交换时抵消。证毕。

docs.title: 10.3 形式的积分与 Stokes 定理
docs.text:
对 \(k\)-形式 \(\omega\) 与奇异 \(k\)-单纯形 \(\sigma\)，定义

\[ \int_\sigma\omega=\int_{\Delta^k}\sigma^*\omega. \]

对链线性延拓。

docs.title: 定理 10.3（Stokes）
docs.text:
若 \(\omega\) 是 \(U\) 上的光滑 \((k-1)\)-形式，\(c\) 是 \(k\)-链，则

\[ \int_{\partial c}\omega=\int_c d\omega. \]

证明思路：先对标准单纯形与单项式形式证明；用 Fubini 定理把边界积分化为累次积分，再用微积分基本定理；最后用 pullback 与链的线性性推广。

特例：

  • \(k=1\)：\(\int_a^b f'(x)dx=f(b)-f(a)\)；
  • \(k=2\)：Green 公式；
  • \(k=3\)：经典 Stokes 与 Gauss 公式。

docs.title: 定理 10.4（Poincaré 引理）
docs.text:
若 \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) 是星形区域，\(\omega\) 是闭 \(k\)-形式（\(k\ge1\)），则存在 \((k-1)\)-形式 \(\eta\) 使

\[ \omega=d\eta. \]

证明状态：暂缓完整证明。构造用径向同伦：沿 \(x\) 到原点的线段积分 \(\omega\)，得到 \(\eta\)；闭性保证 \(d\eta=\omega\)。

推论：在 \(\mathbb R^n\) 中，闭形式局部恰当；全局是否恰当由 de Rham 上同调衡量。

docs.title: 基础
docs.text:
1. 计算 \(d(x\,dy+y\,dz)\)。
  2. 验证 \(d(dx\wedge dy)=0\)。
  3. 写出 \(\mathbb R^2\) 中 Green 公式与 Stokes 定理的对应。

docs.title: 提升
docs.text:
1. 证明 \(d^2=0\)（补全符号抵消）。
  2. 证明 \(\partial^2=0\) 对 \(k=2\) 的情形成立。
  3. 判断 \(\omega=x\,dy-y\,dx\) 在 \(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}\) 上是否恰当。

docs.title: 挑战
docs.text:
1. 证明星形区域上的 Poincaré 引理（写出径向同伦公式）。
  2. 用 Stokes 定理证明：若 \(f\) 在单位圆盘上全纯，则闭路积分为 0（与复分析对照）。

提示：第 6 题计算 \(d\omega\) 并用角度形式说明它不是整体恰当。

docs.title: 第 11 章 · Lebesgue 理论
docs.text: 状态：已展开。给出测度、可测函数、积分与三大收敛定理的完整陈述；证明标为暂缓/提纲。 所属：Rudin 体系 · 第 11 章 · Lebesgue 理论 出处：Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis，第 11 章。

docs.title: 前置
docs.text:
• 第 2 章：拓扑、开集；
  • 第 3 章：级数；
  • 第 6–7 章：积分、一致收敛；
  • 深入理论中的测度概要。

docs.title: 11.1 测度
docs.text:
设 \(\mathcal M\) 是 \(X\) 上的 \(\sigma\)-代数：包含 \(X\)，对补集与可数并封闭。 测度 \(\mu:\mathcal M\to[0,\infty]\) 满足：

  1. \(\mu(\varnothing)=0\)；
  2. 非负性；
  3. 可数可加性：若 \(A_i\) 两两不交，
\[ \mu\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^\infty\mu(A_i). \]

\((X,\mathcal M,\mu)\) 称测度空间。Lebesgue 测度是 \(\mathbb R^n\) 上满足平移不变、规范化的唯一 Borel 测度（在完备化意义下）。

docs.title: 11.2 可测函数
docs.text:
\(f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]\) 可测，若对每个 \(a\in\mathbb R\)，

\[ f^{-1}((a,\infty])\in\mathcal M. \]

等价地，\(\{f>a\}\) 可测对每个 \(a\) 成立。

性质：可测函数的和、积、极限、上确界、下确界仍可测（在避免 \(\infty-\infty\) 的适当条件下）。

docs.title: 定理 11.1（简单函数逼近）
docs.text:
非负可测函数 \(f\) 可写成简单函数列的逐点递增极限：

\[ f=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi_n,\qquad 0\le\phi_1\le\phi_2\le\cdots \]

证明提纲：把值域按 \(2^{-n}\) 分层，截断到 \(n\)，构造 \(\phi_n\)。

docs.title: 11.3 Lebesgue 积分
docs.text:
对非负简单函数 \(\phi=\sum a_i\chi_{A_i}\)，定义

\[ \int\phi\,d\mu=\sum a_i\mu(A_i). \]

对非负可测 \(f\)，定义

\[ \int f\,d\mu=\sup\left\{\int\phi\,d\mu:0\le\phi\le f,\ \phi\text{ 简单}\right\}. \]

对一般可测 \(f\)，写 \(f=f^+-f^-\)；若 \(\int f^+,\int f^-<\infty\)，称 \(f\) 可积，定义

\[ \int f\,d\mu=\int f^+d\mu-\int f^-d\mu. \]

docs.title: 定理 11.2（单调收敛定理，MCT）
docs.text:
若 \(0\le f_n\uparrow f\) 且 \(f_n\) 可测，则

\[ \int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu. \]

证明状态：暂缓完整证明；用简单函数逼近与上确界交换。

docs.title: 定理 11.3（Fatou 引理）
docs.text:
若 \(f_n\ge0\) 可测，则

\[ \int\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu \le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu. \]

证明：对 \(g_n=\inf_{k\ge n}f_k\) 用 MCT，再比较 \(g_n\le f_n\)。

docs.title: 定理 11.4（控制收敛定理，DCT）
docs.text:
若 \(f_n\) 可测，\(f_n\to f\) a.e.，且存在可积 \(g\) 使 \(|f_n|\le g\) a.e.，则

\[ \int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu. \]

证明：对 \(g+f_n\ge0\) 与 \(g-f_n\ge0\) 分别用 Fatou，夹出结论。证毕。

docs.title: 11.4 与 Riemann 积分的关系
docs.text: 若 \(f\) 在 \([a,b]\) 上 Riemann 可积，则 \(f\) Lebesgue 可积，且积分值相同。 反之不成立：Dirichlet 函数 \(\mathbf 1_{\mathbb Q}\) 不是 Riemann 可积，但 Lebesgue 积分为 0（因为 \(\mathbb Q\) 零测）。

docs.title: 定理 11.5（Riemann 可积的 Lebesgue 刻画）
docs.text:
有界 \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) Riemann 可积 \(\iff\) \(f\) 的不连续点集是 Lebesgue 零测集。

证明状态：暂缓完整证明；用振幅函数与零测集定义。

docs.title: 11.5 L² 空间
docs.text:
\[ L^2(\mu)=\left\{f:\int|f|^2\,d\mu<\infty\right\}, \]

配内积

\[ \langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g\,d\mu. \]

docs.title: 定理 11.6（Riesz–Fischer）
docs.text:
\(L^2(\mu)\) 是完备的内积空间（Hilbert 空间）。

证明状态：暂缓；用 Cauchy 列取子列 a.e. 收敛，再用 Fatou 控制。

docs.title: 基础
docs.text:
1. 证明可数集是 Lebesgue 零测集。
  2. 判断 \(\mathbf 1_{\mathbb Q}\) 在 \([0,1]\) 上是否 Riemann 可积、是否 Lebesgue 可积。
  3. 用 MCT 计算 \(\int_0^1\sum_{n\ge1}x^n\,dx\)。

docs.title: 提升
docs.text:
1. 证明 Fatou 引理（由 MCT）。
  2. 证明 DCT（由 Fatou）。
  3. 举例说明 DCT 中“控制函数 \(g\) 可积”不能去掉。

docs.title: 挑战
docs.text:
1. 证明 Riesz–Fischer 定理（可先证 \(L^2\) Cauchy 列有 a.e. 收敛子列）。
  2. 证明：有界函数 Riemann 可积当且仅当不连续点集为零测集。

提示：第 8 题用振幅 \(\omega(x)\) 与集合 \(\{x:\omega(x)\ge1/k\}\)。

docs.title: Mathematics
docs.text:
Mathematics hub. Two entry points: the Classical Academic System and the Educational Stage System; the Classical Academic System itself comprises the Regular System and the Rudin System.

ROUTE A · CLASSICAL Classical Academic System Regular System + Rudin System → ROUTE B · LEARNING Educational Stage System Read by learning stage →

docs.title: Relation Between the Two Systems
docs.text:
Question Which System to Follow I want to study mathematics systematically by topic Classical Academic System → Regular System I want to study chapter by chapter following an analysis textbook Classical Academic System → Rudin System I want to study by year or stage Educational Stage System I am a beginner and do not want to begin with axiomatic set theory Elementary Mathematics within the Educational Stage System I need to fill gaps in rigorous proof, analysis, or algebra Logic, Sets, and Number Systems within the Classical Academic System I am preparing for mathematical competitions Secondary Mathematics → Mathematical Competitions (geometry/algebra/number theory/combinatorics)

Within the Classical Academic System there are the Regular System and the Rudin System; the Educational Stage System is organised by learning stage. All three share the same body of concepts; only the entry points differ.

docs.title: Reading Rules
docs.text:
1. A concept must be defined when it first appears, or linked to a prerequisite page that has already been completed.
  2. Any result used in a proof but not yet established must be reordered, supplied with a proof, or explicitly marked "proof deferred".
  3. Equivalence relations before quotient sets, mappings before isomorphisms, order relations before suprema.
  4. Theory pages answer "what does this depend on"; stage pages answer "how to study, and why the material is ordered this way".
  5. What is offered here is a knowledge map and a study order, not a complete textbook; every page can be extended with further definitions, theorems, and exercises.

docs.title: Study Rules
docs.text:
This page specifies how the site organizes its content, so that "nothing later on suddenly introduces something not explained earlier".

The table of contents is only a map; the actual prerequisite constraints must be imposed on every page.

docs.title: 1. Two Orders, Not to Be Mixed
docs.text:
Order Question Answered Where Used Proof order What must already be in place in order to prove this result? Theory pages Learning order What should one ideally have gone through in order to understand this concept? Educational stage pages

A theory page may not substitute "studied in secondary school" for a definition; a stage page may begin with intuition, but must state "for the rigorous definition, see the theory page".

docs.title: 2. Every Page Must State Its Prerequisites
docs.text:
Theory pages begin with the following fixed text:

1Prerequisites: logic and sets; sets, mappings, equivalence relations.
2Not used on this page: groups, topology, measure.

Stage pages begin with the following fixed text:

1Prerequisites: similar triangles, basic properties of circles.
2Not yet required: axiomatic set theory, construction of the real numbers.

docs.title: 3. Define on First Occurrence
docs.text:
• When a new concept appears for the first time, give a definition or link to a page where it is defined;
  • do not replace a definition with "obviously" or "as is well known";
  • the meaning of a symbol must be explained at its first occurrence (e.g. \(\mathbb N,\mathbb R,\mathcal P(A)\)).

docs.title: 4. Handling Incomplete Prerequisites
docs.text:
If a proof requires a result not yet established, one may only:

  1. Reorder: first supply the prerequisites;
  2. Supply the proof: give a complete proof on this page;
  3. Defer the proof: explicitly write "this page does not prove it, and only uses the conclusion", and list the required prerequisites.

Not permitted:

  • treating a conclusion as a definition;
  • proving a conclusion by means of a proposition equivalent to it;
  • using advanced theorems without indicating their source.

docs.title: 5. Dependency Constraints
docs.text:
The following orders may not be exchanged:

First Then Reason Equivalence relations Quotient sets The elements of a quotient set are equivalence classes Mappings Isomorphisms An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism Order relations Supremum The supremum is defined in terms of order Natural numbers/induction Recursive definitions Recursion depends on the structure of the natural numbers Completeness of the reals Limit theorems The existence of limits depends on completeness Metric spaces General topology Topology abstracts the structure of open sets Groups/rings/fields Quotient groups/quotient rings/field extensions Quotient structures depend on equivalence relations and homomorphisms

docs.title: Theory Page
docs.text:
1. Prerequisites;
  2. Core objects;
  3. Definitions;
  4. Theorems and proofs (or proof outlines/deferred proofs);
  5. Typical examples and counterexamples;
  6. Dependency remarks;
  7. Downward connections;
  8. Checkpoints.

docs.title: Stage Page
docs.text:
1. Stage objectives;
  2. Module order;
  3. What each module "explains clearly";
  4. Connection to the next stage;
  5. Checkpoints (explanation/computation/proof).

docs.title: Competition Page
docs.text:
1. Prerequisites;
  2. Core results and proofs;
  3. Method-based worked examples;
  4. Graded exercises;
  5. Hints and solutions;
  6. Summary of methods.

docs.title: 7. Naming and Notation
docs.text:
• Sets: \(A,B,X,Y\); elements: \(x,y\);
  • Natural numbers: \(\mathbb N\); integers: \(\mathbb Z\); rational numbers: \(\mathbb Q\); real numbers: \(\mathbb R\); complex numbers: \(\mathbb C\);
  • Mappings: \(f:X\to Y\); composition: \(g\circ f\);
  • Groups: \(G\); fields: \(F\); vector spaces: \(V\);
  • Metrics: \(d(x,y)\); norms: \(\|x\|\); inner products: \(\langle x,y\rangle\).

The same symbol may have different meanings on different pages, and its meaning must be explained at its first occurrence within a page.

docs.title: 8. Correspondence Between the Two Tracks
docs.text: Educational Stage Theoretical Layer Remarks Elementary Mathematics Intuitive part of number systems Use numbers first, do not construct them first Secondary Mathematics (Foundations) Number systems Real numbers understood via the number line Secondary Mathematics (Advanced) Layers 1–2 and 4 Proofs, mappings, vectors Mathematical Competitions Logical methods + special topics Not required to complete all of secondary mathematics University General Foundations Layer 4–5 computations May proceed in parallel with theory Professional Core Layers 5–6 Rigorous analysis, algebra, topology Advanced Topics Advanced Prerequisites listed per topic

docs.title: 9. Quality Check
docs.text:
Check each page before publication:

  • [ ] Are the prerequisites clearly stated?
  • [ ] Are new concepts defined?
  • [ ] Does any proof cite an unestablished result?
  • [ ] Is the notation explained?
  • [ ] Do the worked examples actually use the methods of this section?
  • [ ] Does a stage page mark the boundary between "intuitive" and "rigorous"?

docs.text: This site is a study compilation, not a reproduction of the original texts. Definitions, theorems, and proofs are rewritten according to standard textbooks; the reference sources are listed below.

docs.text:

  • Wikipedia: Used to verify definitions, theorem names, and standard formulations; the main text relies primarily on textbook-style proofs.
  • Deferred proofs: Explicitly marked in Proof Status; citations are not treated as proofs.
  • If an exposition is found to be inconsistent with the textbooks, the standard textbook formulation takes precedence, and the discrepancy is noted on the page.

docs.title: Educational Stage System · Overview
docs.text:
Organized around how a learner comes to understand mathematics step by step: starting from concrete quantities, figures, and real problems, and gradually entering symbols, functions, change, and abstract structures.

It does not replace the theoretical system; rather, the two are two ways of reading the same knowledge base.

docs.title: Three Main Entry Points
docs.text:
Entry Subtitle Goal Typical Starting Point Elementary Mathematics Foundational Introduction Understand number, operations, measurement, and basic figures, and be able to explain "why the calculation works" Quantity, counting, addition and subtraction Secondary Mathematics Secondary School Stage Move from arithmetic to algebra, functions, geometric proof, and randomness Rational numbers, algebraic expressions, equations University Mathematics University and Beyond University general foundation → major core → advanced topics Calculus, linear algebra, discrete mathematics

"Elementary/Secondary/University" here denotes a learning stage, not a ranking of mathematical value; the traditional "elementary mathematics" also contains a large amount of secondary-school content, so the pages are also labelled "Foundational Introduction/Secondary School Stage/University and Beyond".

docs.title: The Four Modules of Secondary Mathematics
docs.text:
Module Main Content Role Foundation Stage Real numbers, algebraic expressions, equations and inequalities, introduction to functions, plane geometry, foundations of probability and statistics Establish the foundations of secondary-school mathematics Deepening Stage Functions, trigonometry, vectors, analytic geometry, sequences, advanced probability and statistics Systematic expansion of knowledge Mathematical Competitions Geometry, Algebra, Number Theory, Combinatorics Topic-based exploration, problem-solving methods, and proof training University Transition Intuition for limits, rates of change, first steps in derivatives, accumulation of area Preparation for university mathematics

The competition module has its own entry point, but shares the same set of prerequisite rules: once similar triangles have been studied, one may enter introductory competition geometry; once divisibility and factors have been studied, one may enter competition number theory.

docs.title: Correspondence with the Theoretical System
docs.text: Educational Stage Corresponding Theoretical Layer Explanation Elementary Mathematics The intuitive part of number systems: "natural numbers, integers, rational numbers" Use numbers first, do not construct them first Secondary Mathematics: Foundation Number systems within the number-system layer; preliminary set language of sets Real numbers are first understood through the number line and operations Secondary Mathematics: Deepening Proof in logic; mappings in sets; vectors in algebra Proof training appears gradually Mathematical Competitions Logical methods + special topics in number theory/combinatorics/geometry/algebra Does not require completing all secondary-school content University Mathematics: General Foundation Computation and applications of layers 4–5 May proceed in parallel with the theoretical route University Mathematics: Major Core Rigorous theory of layers 5–6 Mathematical analysis, abstract algebra, topology Advanced Topics In depth Prerequisites listed per topic

docs.title: A Recommended Main Line
docs.text:
Quantity and operations → symbols and relations → functions and spaces → change and randomness → abstract structures and rigorous theory.

This main line is not a mandatory queue. The university general foundation (calculus, linear algebra, probability) may be taken in parallel; a learner majoring in mathematics may choose the rigorous analysis route directly, without first completing a computation-oriented calculus course.

docs.title: Page Structure
docs.text:
Every stage page answers the same questions:

  1. The goals of this stage;
  2. Module order and internal order;
  3. What each module "should make clear";
  4. Articulation with the next stage;
  5. Checkpoints: what one can explain, compute, and prove.

docs.title: Entry Points
docs.text:
• Elementary Mathematics · Foundational Introduction
  • Secondary Mathematics · Secondary School Stage
  • Mathematical Competitions · Topic-Based Exploration
  • University Mathematics · University and Beyond

docs.title: Mathematical Competitions · Topic Extensions
docs.text: Scope: an independent extension module within Secondary Mathematics, standing alongside the foundation stage and the deepening stage. Objective: to deepen the capacity for problem analysis and proof; entry is possible once the corresponding prerequisites are in place, and it is not necessary to complete all of Secondary Mathematics first.

docs.title: The Four Topics
docs.text:
Topic Introductory Content Core Content Advanced Content Geometry Angle chasing, congruence and similarity, area relations, basic properties of circles Collinearity and concurrence, power of a point and radical axis, Menelaus' theorem and Ceva's theorem, homothety and rotation Spiral similarity, inversion, special points of a triangle and combined configurations Algebra Factorization, manipulation of identities, completing the square, Vieta's formulas, the basic inequality Polynomials, symmetric expressions, proof of inequalities, sequences and recurrences, functional equations Polynomial interpolation, analysis of roots, complex functional equations, combined problems on parameters and extrema Number Theory Divisibility, primes, greatest common divisor, Euclidean algorithm, fundamental theorem of arithmetic Congruences, linear Diophantine equations, modular arithmetic, Fermat's little theorem, Euler's theorem, Chinese remainder theorem Orders and primitive roots, p-adic valuation, quadratic residues, Diophantine equations and infinite descent Combinatorics Addition and multiplication principles, permutations and combinations, enumeration by cases, pigeonhole principle Double counting, inclusion–exclusion principle, recurrences, invariants and monotone quantities, extremal principle, basics of graph theory Construction and existence, coloring and covering, combinatorial identities, generating functions, combined graph-theory problems

These are suggested levels of study; they do not correspond directly to the official syllabus of any particular competition. Each topic should state its prerequisites explicitly: before studying generating functions, for instance, one should first possess a foundation in polynomials and the corresponding formal manipulations.

docs.title: Shared Methodological Foundations
docs.text:
Before the four topics, a shared unit on the "foundations of competition methods" is established:

  • direct proof, proof by contradiction, mathematical induction;
  • case analysis;
  • construction of counterexamples;
  • formulation of conjectures from small-scale examples;
  • translation of verbal conditions into algebraic, geometric, or counting language.

Methods such as infinite descent and the extremal principle are developed within the relevant topics in connection with specific problems, so as to avoid an accumulation of abstract techniques at the outset.

docs.title: Page Structure
docs.text:
Each topic page is organized uniformly in the following order:

  1. Prerequisites: what one should be able to do before entering the topic;
  2. Core Results and Proofs: theorems, lemmas, standard models;
  3. Worked Examples by Method: classified by method, not merely by problem type;
  4. Tiered Exercises: foundational consolidation / topic enhancement / comprehensive challenge;
  5. Hints and Solutions: hints first, then the complete proof;
  6. Method Summary: when to use a method, why to use it, and the conditions under which it fails.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text: Prerequisites: congruence, similarity, basic properties of circles, area formulas. Objective: to move from "looking at a figure to find relations" to "organizing a proof by means of theorems".

docs.title: Introductory
docs.text: Method Key Point Angle chasing Introduce unknown angles and transfer them by means of parallel lines, isosceles triangles, and cyclic quadrilaterals Congruence and similarity Identify corresponding sides and angles; attend to the order of correspondence Area relations For triangles of equal height, the ratio of areas equals the ratio of bases; for similar figures, the ratio of areas equals the square of the similarity ratio Basic properties of circles Inscribed angles, central angles, tangents, tangent–chord angles

docs.title: Menelaus' Theorem
docs.text:
In \(\triangle ABC\), let a line meet \(BC,CA,AB\) (or their extensions) at \(D,E,F\) respectively; then

\[ \frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}\cdot\frac{AF}{FB}=1 \]

(the directed-segment version carries signs). It is used to prove that three points are collinear.

docs.title: Ceva's Theorem
docs.text:
In \(\triangle ABC\), if \(AD,BE,CF\) are concurrent, then

\[ \frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}\cdot\frac{AF}{FB}=1. \]

The converse theorem is used to prove that three lines are concurrent.

docs.title: Power of a Point and Radical Axis
docs.text:
The power of a point \(P\) with respect to a circle \(O\):

\[ \operatorname{Pow}(P)=PO^2-r^2. \]

If a secant through \(P\) meets the circle at \(A,B\), then \(PA\cdot PB=\operatorname{Pow}(P)\) (directed version). The radical axis of two circles is the locus of points having equal powers with respect to the two circles; the radical axis is perpendicular to the line of centers.

docs.title: Homothety and Rotation
docs.text:
• Homothety: preserves angles and scales lengths proportionally;
  • Rotation: preserves lengths and angles; frequently used to construct equilateral triangles and squares;
  • Rotational similarity (spiral similarity): a rotation followed by a homothety; a standard tool for problems involving "a common point together with a ratio".

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
• Inversion: with a circle as the unit, transforms lines and circles into one another; treats tangency and concyclicity problems;
  • Special points of a triangle: centroid, circumcenter, incenter, orthocenter, nine-point circle;
  • Combined configurations: combining angles, ratios, and powers of a point.

docs.title: Worked Example (Method Illustration)
docs.text:
Problem: In \(\triangle ABC\), let \(D\in BC\), \(E\in CA\), \(F\in AB\), and suppose \(AD,BE,CF\) are concurrent. Given \(BD/DC=2/3\) and \(CE/EA=3/4\), find \(AF/FB\).

By Ceva's theorem:

\[ \frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}\cdot\frac{AF}{FB}=1 \]

Substituting:

\[ \frac23\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac{AF}{FB}=1 \Rightarrow \frac{AF}{FB}=2. \]

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Foundational: use inscribed angles to prove that the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
  2. Enhancement: use Menelaus' theorem to prove that three points are collinear.
  3. Challenge: use the radical axis to prove that the line joining the intersection points of two circles is perpendicular to the line of centers.

docs.title: Method Summary
docs.text:
• First identify the structure — "collinear / concurrent / concyclic" — then choose the theorem;
  • For ratio problems, consider Menelaus' theorem, Ceva's theorem, and similarity first;
  • For circle problems, consider the power of a point, the radical axis, and inscribed angles first;
  • Do not rely solely on adding auxiliary lines; first determine the target structure.

docs.title: Algebra
docs.text: Prerequisites: factorization, multiplication formulas, quadratic equations in one variable, Vieta's formulas, the basic inequality. Objective: to translate conditions into algebraic relations and to organize proofs by means of identities and inequalities.

docs.title: Introductory
docs.text:
• Factorization: common factor extraction, formula method, grouping, cross multiplication;
  • Completing the square: \(a^2\pm2ab+b^2=(a\pm b)^2\);
  • Vieta's formulas: if \(x_1,x_2\) are the roots of \(ax^2+bx+c=0\), then [ x_1+x_2=-\frac ba,\qquad x_1x_2=\frac ca. ]
  • The basic inequality: \(a^2+b^2\ge2ab\), and for \(a,b>0\), \(\frac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab}\).

docs.title: Polynomials
docs.text:
• Remainder theorem: the remainder on dividing \(f(x)\) by \(x-a\) is \(f(a)\);
  • Factor theorem: \(f(a)=0\iff x-a\mid f(x)\);
  • Rational root theorem: a rational root \(p/q\) of a polynomial with integer coefficients satisfies \(p\mid a_0,\ q\mid a_n\).

docs.title: Symmetric Expressions
docs.text:
A symmetric polynomial can be expressed in terms of the elementary symmetric expressions:

\[ s_1=x_1+x_2,\qquad s_2=x_1x_2. \]

In the three-variable case, use \(s_1=x+y+z,\ s_2=xy+yz+zx,\ s_3=xyz\).

docs.title: Proof of Inequalities
docs.text:
Standard methods:

  1. taking differences or ratios;
  2. completing the square;
  3. the AM–GM inequality;
  4. Cauchy–Schwarz;
  5. the rearrangement inequality;
  6. smoothing / local modification.

docs.title: Sequences and Recurrences
docs.text:
• summation of arithmetic and geometric sequences;
  • telescoping;
  • the characteristic equation for linear recurrences;
  • generating functions (advanced).

docs.title: Functional Equations
docs.text: First substitute special values (\(0,1,-1\)), then guess the form, and finally verify it. Attend to additional conditions such as the domain, continuity, and monotonicity.

docs.title: Worked Example (Method Illustration)
docs.text:
Problem: Positive numbers \(a,b,c\) satisfy \(abc=1\). Prove that

\[ a+b+c\ge3. \]

By AM–GM:

\[ \frac{a+b+c}{3}\ge\sqrt[3]{abc}=1, \]

hence \(a+b+c\ge3\), with equality if and only if \(a=b=c=1\).

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Foundational: use Vieta's formulas to find the sum of the squares of the two roots.
  2. Enhancement: prove that \(a^2+b^2+c^2\ge ab+bc+ca\).
  3. Challenge: use smoothing to prove the maximum of the product for a given sum.

docs.title: Method Summary
docs.text:
• First examine the structure: symmetry, cyclicity, degree, domain;
  • Complete the square when possible; factorize when possible;
  • For inequalities, attend to the equality conditions;
  • For functional equations, substitute special values first, then verify.

docs.title: Number Theory
docs.text: Prerequisites: divisibility, primes, greatest common divisor, Euclidean algorithm, fundamental theorem of arithmetic. Objective: to treat integer problems by means of congruences, factorization, and structure theorems.

docs.title: Introductory
docs.text:
• Divisibility: \(a\mid b\iff b=ak\);
  • Euclidean algorithm: \(\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b,a\bmod b)\);
  • Fundamental theorem of arithmetic: uniqueness of prime factorization;
  • Greatest common divisor and least common multiple: \(\gcd(a,b)\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)=ab\).

docs.title: Congruences
docs.text: \(a\equiv b\pmod m\iff m\mid(a-b)\). Congruences may be added, subtracted, and multiplied; division requires care, and one may cancel \(c\) only when \(\gcd(c,m)=1\).

docs.title: Linear Diophantine Equations
docs.text:
\[ ax+by=c \]

has an integer solution if and only if \(\gcd(a,b)\mid c\). The general solution is given by a particular solution plus the homogeneous solution \( (b/g,\,-a/g)t \).

docs.title: Fermat's Little Theorem and Euler's Theorem
docs.text:
If \(p\) is prime and \(p\nmid a\), then

\[ a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p. \]

If \(\gcd(a,m)=1\), then

\[ a^{\varphi(m)}\equiv1\pmod m. \]

docs.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem
docs.text:
If \(m_1,\dots,m_k\) are pairwise coprime, then the system of congruences

\[ x\equiv a_i\pmod{m_i} \]

has a unique solution modulo \(M=\prod m_i\).

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
• orders and primitive roots;
  • quadratic residues and the Legendre symbol;
  • the p-adic valuation \(v_p(n)\);
  • infinite descent for Diophantine equations;
  • the Pell equation.

docs.title: Worked Example (Method Illustration)
docs.text:
Problem: Find \(3^{100}\bmod 7\).

By Fermat's little theorem, \(3^6\equiv1\pmod7\). Since \(100=6\cdot16+4\),

\[ 3^{100}\equiv3^4=81\equiv4\pmod7. \]

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Foundational: use the Euclidean algorithm to find \(\gcd(252,198)\).
  2. Enhancement: solve \(7x\equiv3\pmod{11}\).
  3. Challenge: use the Chinese remainder theorem to solve three congruences.

docs.title: Method Summary
docs.text:
• First examine the modulus: prime, coprime, or a power;
  • Large exponents → reduction by Fermat's little theorem or Euler's theorem;
  • Linear equations → test by gcd;
  • Multiple moduli → CRT;
  • Diophantine equations → factorization, congruence restrictions, infinite descent.

docs.title: Combinatorics
docs.text: Prerequisites: addition and multiplication principles, permutations and combinations, enumeration by cases, pigeonhole principle. Objective: to turn "counting" and "existence" into provable arguments.

docs.title: Introductory
docs.text:
• Addition principle: the classes are disjoint and exhaustive;
  • Multiplication principle: stepwise counting;
  • Permutations \(P(n,k)=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\) and combinations \(\binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\);
  • Pigeonhole principle: if \(n+1\) objects are placed into \(n\) boxes, then at least one box contains 2 objects.

docs.title: Double Counting
docs.text:
Count the same set in two ways to obtain an identity. For example:

\[ \sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk=2^n \]

(by classifying according to subset size, or by choosing or not choosing each element).

docs.title: Inclusion–Exclusion Principle
docs.text: [ |A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|, ] [ \left|\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i\right| =\sum|A_i|-\sum|A_i\cap A_j|+\cdots+(-1)^{n+1}|A_1\cap\cdots\cap A_n|. ]

docs.title: Recurrences
docs.text:
Reduce the case \(n\) to the case \(n-1\) (or smaller), attending to the initial conditions. For example, the Fibonacci sequence:

\[ F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2},\quad F_0=0,\ F_1=1. \]

docs.title: Invariants and Monotone Quantities
docs.text: Assign a quantity to a process and prove that it is invariant or monotone under the operations, thereby excluding certain terminal states.

docs.title: Extremal Principle
docs.text: Consider the largest or smallest, the most or the fewest, and boundary cases, and derive a contradiction or a structure from the extremal object.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
• construction and existence: guess first, then construct, and finally prove that the conditions are satisfied;
  • coloring and covering: use a color invariant to disprove a covering;
  • combinatorial identities: double counting, generating functions;
  • graph theory: trees, matchings, Eulerian circuits, an introduction to Ramsey theory.

docs.title: Worked Example (Method Illustration)
docs.text:
Problem: Prove that among \(n\) people at least two share a birth month (\(n=13\)).

A year has only 12 months; place the 13 people into 12 "boxes" according to their birth month. By the pigeonhole principle, at least one box contains 2 people.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Foundational: use inclusion–exclusion to find the number of integers from 1 to 100 that are divisible by neither 2 nor 3.
  2. Enhancement: use double counting to prove that \(\sum k\binom nk=n2^{n-1}\).
  3. Challenge: use an invariant to prove a coloring problem.

docs.title: Method Summary
docs.text:
• First decide whether the problem concerns "counting" or "existence";
  • Counting: classification, stepwise counting, inclusion–exclusion, double counting;
  • Existence: pigeonhole, extremal principle, invariants, construction;
  • Check for "no overlap and no omission" and for boundary cases.

docs.title: Elementary Mathematics · Foundations and Initiation
docs.text:
Objective: to understand numbers, operations, measurement and basic figures, to be able to explain the meaning of a calculation, and to solve simple practical problems.

This stage does not presuppose set theory, axioms or the construction of number systems; the emphasis is on building notions of quantity and space from concrete experience.

docs.title: Module Overview
docs.text:
Order Module Main Content and Internal Order 1 Quantity and Natural Numbers Classification and correspondence → counting → zero and the natural numbers → comparison of numbers → place value and the decimal system 2 Addition and Subtraction Combining and increasing → decreasing and comparing → addition and subtraction as inverse operations → computation and estimation 3 Multiplication and Division Grouping into equal quantities → multiplication → equal sharing and quotative division → multiplication and division as inverse operations → remainders 4 Laws of Operation Commutative, associative and distributive laws → brackets → mixed arithmetic of the four operations 5 Measurement and Basic Figures Units of length, time, mass, etc. → segments and angles → common plane figures and solid figures 6 Factors and Multiples Divisibility → factors and multiples → odd and even numbers, primes and composites → common factors and common multiples 7 Fractions and Decimals The unit whole and equal parts → comparison and equivalence of fractions → operations on fractions → conversion between decimals and fractions 8 Ratios, Rates and Percentages Multiplicative relations → ratios and the unit quantity → percentages → discounts, growth and simple proportional problems 9 Perimeter, Area and Volume Units of length, area and volume → measurement → computation for common figures 10 Introductory Algebra and Data Unknowns and simple equalities → simple equations; classification of data → statistical charts → the mean

These modules need not be followed in strictly serial order. Length measurement may be combined with the study of addition and subtraction; area may be understood by means of grids when multiplication is studied.

docs.title: 1. Quantity and Natural Numbers
docs.text:
• Counting is not the recitation of a chant but one-to-one correspondence;
  • zero means "none", and it is also a number;
  • place-value notation: the same digit denotes different magnitudes in different positions;
  • comparing magnitudes: first compare the number of digits, then compare the higher places.

docs.title: 2. Addition and Subtraction
docs.text:
• Addition: combining, increasing, counting on;
  • Subtraction: taking away, comparing, finding one part from a known sum and the other part;
  • addition and subtraction are inverse operations: \(a+b=c\iff c-b=a\);
  • estimation: first judge the order of magnitude, then decide whether an exact computation is required.

docs.title: 3. Multiplication and Division
docs.text:
• Multiplication: a concise notation for equal addends;
  • Division: equal sharing and quotative division are two models;
  • remainder: \(a=bq+r,\ 0\le r<b\);
  • multiplication and division are inverse operations, but division by zero is meaningless.

docs.title: 4. Laws of Operation
docs.text:
[ a+b=b+a,\qquad ab=ba, ] [ (a+b)+c=a+(b+c),\qquad (ab)c=a(bc), ] [ a(b+c)=ab+ac. ]

Brackets change the order of operations; mixed arithmetic of the four operations proceeds by "multiplication and division first, addition and subtraction afterwards, with brackets taking precedence".

docs.title: 5. Measurement and Basic Figures
docs.text:
• Unit conversion: units of length, area and volume differ, and so do their conversion rates;
  • segment, ray, line;
  • angles: acute, right, obtuse, straight and full angles;
  • plane figures: triangle, quadrilateral, circle;
  • solid figures: cuboid, cube, cylinder, cone, sphere.

docs.title: 6. Factors and Multiples
docs.text:
• divisibility: \(a\mid b\) means that there exists an integer \(k\) with \(b=ak\);
  • factors and multiples occur in pairs;
  • a prime is a natural number greater than 1 whose only positive factors are 1 and itself;
  • common factors, greatest common factor, common multiples, least common multiple.

docs.title: 7. Fractions and Decimals
docs.text:
• a fraction is "a number of equal parts taken after dividing the unit whole into equal parts";
  • equivalent fractions: \(\frac12=\frac24\);
  • addition and subtraction of fractions require a common denominator; multiplication is "numerator times numerator, denominator times denominator", and division is "multiplication by the reciprocal";
  • a decimal is a decimal fraction; finite decimals and infinite repeating decimals can be converted into fractions.

Why is division by a fraction equal to multiplication by its reciprocal? Because \(\frac{a}{b}\div\frac{c}{d}\) denotes "how many \(\frac{c}{d}\) are contained in \(\frac{a}{b}\)", that is,

\[ \frac{a}{b}\div\frac{c}{d}=\frac{a}{b}\cdot\frac{d}{c}. \]

docs.title: 8. Ratios, Rates and Percentages
docs.text:
• the ratio \(a:b\) expresses the multiplicative relation between two quantities;
  • if both the antecedent and the consequent of a ratio are multiplied or divided by the same nonzero number, the value of the ratio is unchanged;
  • a percentage is a ratio with denominator 100;
  • discounts, growth rates and interest rates are all applications of percentages.

docs.title: 9. Perimeter, Area and Volume
docs.text:
• the perimeter is the length of the boundary; the area is the number of unit squares occupied by a plane figure; the volume is the number of unit cubes occupied by a solid figure;
  • area of a rectangle \(S=ab\), of a parallelogram \(S=ah\), of a triangle \(S=\frac12 ah\), of a circle \(S=\pi r^2\);
  • area formulas should be derived by dissection, subdivision or unit squares, not merely memorised.

docs.title: 10. Introductory Algebra and Data
docs.text:
• use letters to denote unknowns or varying quantities;
  • simple equations: \(x+3=8\), subtract 3 from both sides;
  • classification of data, frequency, bar/line/pie charts;
  • mean = sum ÷ number of items, which is easily affected by extreme values.

docs.title: Teaching Principles
docs.text:
1. Concrete before symbolic: use objects, figures and the number line to explain operations;
  2. Meaning before algorithm: first explain "why the computation is done this way", then practise speed;
  3. Allow informal language: first let students explain in their own words, then gradually introduce standard terminology;
  4. Do not impose axioms prematurely: this stage does not require set theory, the Peano axioms or a construction of the real numbers.

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
• Can explain why division by a fraction is multiplication by its reciprocal, rather than merely reciting the rule.
  • Can explain area formulas by means of unit squares.
  • Can determine whether a number is prime, and find the greatest common factor / least common multiple.
  • Can read simple statistical charts and describe situations in which the mean may be misleading.

docs.title: Secondary Mathematics · Secondary School Stage
docs.text:
From arithmetic towards algebra, functions and reasoning. Internally it distinguishes a "Foundation Stage" and a "Deepening Stage", corresponding to the natural transition from lower-secondary to upper-secondary knowledge, but it is not tied to the specific year of any region.

Mathematical competitions are a separate extension module; see Mathematical Competitions.

docs.title: Module Overview
docs.text:
Stage Study Module Main Content and Internal Order Foundation Rational Numbers and Real Numbers Negative numbers → the number line → absolute value → operations on rational numbers → square roots and irrational numbers → real numbers Foundation Algebraic Expressions Letters denoting numbers → operations on integral expressions → multiplication formulas → factorisation → fractional expressions and the conditions for them Foundation Equations and Inequalities Linear equation in one unknown → systems of equations → linear inequality in one unknown → quadratic equation in one unknown Foundation Coordinates and Introduction to Functions Cartesian coordinate plane → relations between variables → functions and their graphs → linear functions → inverse proportional functions → quadratic functions Foundation Plane Geometry and Proof Relations among basic figures → propositions and proof → congruence of triangles → quadrilaterals → similarity → Pythagorean theorem → circles Foundation Data and Randomness Data distributions → measures of central tendency and dispersion → awareness of sampling → simple random events and probability Deepening Sets and the Language of Logic Sets and intervals → conditions and conclusions → necessary and sufficient conditions → universal and existential statements Deepening Systematic Study of Functions Domain and range → monotonicity, even/odd symmetry → composition and inverse functions, preliminary → exponential and logarithmic functions Deepening Trigonometric Functions Similarity and trigonometric ratios in right triangles → radians and the unit circle → trigonometric functions → identities and solving triangles Deepening Vectors and Geometry Vector operations and coordinates → scalar product → equations of lines and circles → conic sections; spatial position and solid geometry Deepening Sequences and Discrete Methods Sequences → arithmetic and geometric sequences → summation → mathematical induction; counting principles → permutations and combinations Deepening Advanced Probability and Statistics Conditional probability and independence → discrete random variables → expectation and variance → common discrete distributions and statistical applications Transition Rate of Change and Intuition for Limits Average rate of change → secants and tangents → infinite approximation → first steps in derivatives and intuition for accumulated area

"Real numbers" are understood here mainly through the number line, radicals and the properties of operations; Dedekind cuts need not be completed first; "sets" first serve as a language for expressing the range of objects, and set-theoretic axiomatics is not developed immediately.

docs.title: Rational Numbers and Real Numbers
docs.text:
• Negative numbers are quantities of opposite meaning; the number line correlates numbers with positions;
  • absolute value is the distance to the origin;
  • a rational number can be written as \(\frac pq\) (\(p,q\in\mathbb Z,\ q\ne0\));
  • \(\sqrt2\) is not a rational number (proof by contradiction: assume \(\sqrt2=p/q\) in lowest terms and derive a contradiction);
  • real numbers = rational numbers + irrational numbers; real numbers correspond one-to-one with the points of the number line (intuitive version).

docs.title: Algebraic Expressions
docs.text:
• letters denote numbers; operations on integral expressions obey the commutative, associative and distributive laws;
  • multiplication formulas: [ (a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2,\quad (a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2, ] [ a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b); ]
  • factorisation is the reverse use of the multiplication formulas;
  • the condition for a fractional expression to be meaningful: the denominator is nonzero.

docs.title: Equations and Inequalities
docs.text:
• linear equation in one unknown: transposition of terms, collection of like terms, reduction of the coefficient to one;
  • systems of equations: elimination by substitution, elimination by addition and subtraction;
  • linear inequality in one unknown: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the sign;
  • quadratic equation in one unknown: factorisation, completing the square, the quadratic formula [ x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}. ]

The discriminant \(\Delta=b^2-4ac\) determines the number of real roots.

docs.title: Coordinates and Introduction to Functions
docs.text:
• Cartesian coordinate plane: ordered pairs \((x,y)\);
  • function: each independent variable \(x\) corresponds to a unique \(y\);
  • linear function \(y=kx+b\): the graph is a line, and \(k\) is the slope;
  • inverse proportional function \(y=k/x\): the graph is a hyperbola;
  • quadratic function \(y=ax^2+bx+c\): the graph is a parabola, with vertex and axis of symmetry.

docs.title: Plane Geometry and Proof
docs.text:
• propositions, conditions, conclusions;
  • congruent triangles: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL;
  • similar triangles: AA, SAS, SSS;
  • Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle, \(a^2+b^2=c^2\);
  • circles: central angles, inscribed angles, tangents, chords.

Proof training begins here: every step must have a justification (a definition, an axiom, or an already-proved theorem); it is not enough that a figure looks correct.

docs.title: Data and Randomness
docs.text:
• mean, median, mode;
  • variance/standard deviation measure dispersion;
  • sampling must be representative;
  • simple probability: number of favourable outcomes / total number of outcomes (in the equally likely case).

docs.title: Sets and the Language of Logic
docs.text:
• sets, intervals, union/intersection/complement;
  • sufficient conditions, necessary conditions, necessary and sufficient conditions;
  • universal quantifier and existential quantifier;
  • negation of a proposition.

docs.title: Systematic Study of Functions
docs.text:
• domain, range;
  • monotonicity, even/odd symmetry, periodicity;
  • composite functions and inverse functions;
  • exponential functions, logarithmic functions, and the inverse relation between them.

docs.title: Trigonometric Functions
docs.text:
• sine, cosine and tangent in a right triangle;
  • radian measure and the unit circle;
  • \(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1\);
  • addition formulas, double-angle formulas;
  • the law of sines and the law of cosines for solving triangles.

docs.title: Vectors and Geometry
docs.text:
• vector addition, scalar multiplication, coordinate representation;
  • scalar product \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta\);
  • equations of lines and circles;
  • conic sections: ellipse, hyperbola, parabola;
  • spatial vectors and solid geometry.

docs.title: Sequences and Discrete Methods
docs.text:
• arithmetic sequences, geometric sequences;
  • summation formulas;
  • mathematical induction;
  • counting principles, permutations and combinations.

docs.title: Advanced Probability and Statistics
docs.text:
• conditional probability \(P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)\);
  • independence \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\);
  • discrete random variables, expectation, variance;
  • binomial distribution, geometric distribution, and others.

docs.title: University Transition
docs.text:
• average rate of change \(\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}h\);
  • slope of a secant → slope of a tangent;
  • the intuition of infinite approximation;
  • accumulation of area and the intuition of the definite integral.

This stage establishes intuition only; it does not replace the university \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definitions and rigorous proofs.

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
• Can prove by contradiction that \(\sqrt2\) is irrational.
  • Can determine sufficient/necessary conditions and write down their negations.
  • Can complete a geometric proof, giving a justification for every step.
  • Can state the intuitive meaning of the derivative and of the definite integral, rather than merely memorising formulas.

docs.title: University Mathematics · Undergraduate and Advanced
docs.text: We adopt "university mathematics" in the broad sense: it encompasses several directions of university mathematics, not merely the calculus course. Internally it is divided into "university common foundation → disciplinary core → advanced topics"; the common foundation may be studied in parallel.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Stage Course or Module Main Content Main Prerequisites University Common Foundation Single-Variable Calculus Limits, continuity, derivatives, integrals, elementary differential equations, series Functions, algebra, trigonometry University Common Foundation Linear Algebra Systems of equations, matrices, vector spaces, linear maps, eigenvalues, orthogonality Algebraic operations, coordinates and vectors University Common Foundation Multivariable Calculus Partial derivatives, multiple integrals, line and surface integrals Single-variable calculus, solid geometry; relevant linear algebra University Common Foundation Discrete Mathematics and Proof Logic, sets, relations, induction, combinatorics, graph theory Secondary-school algebra, basic proof awareness University Common Foundation Probability and Statistics Random variables, distributions, expectation, estimation, testing, and regression Secondary-school probability; continuous distributions require integration Disciplinary Core Mathematical Analysis and Real Analysis Rigorous limits and continuity, completeness, sequences of functions and convergence Proof methods, sets and mappings, calculus experience Disciplinary Core Abstract Algebra Groups, rings, fields, and maps between structures Sets, relations, proofs, linear algebra experience Disciplinary Core Foundations of Geometry and Topology Metric spaces, topological spaces, foundations of curves and surfaces Relevant content from analysis and linear algebra Disciplinary Core Differential Equations and Numerical Methods Ordinary differential equations, approximate solution, error and stability Calculus, linear algebra Advanced Topics Advanced Theory and Applications Measure theory, complex analysis, functional analysis, differential geometry, optimization, stochastic processes, etc. Specified separately for each topic

docs.title: University Common Foundation
docs.text: This layer may be studied in parallel; it need not be arranged as "finish all of calculus, then study linear algebra, then study probability".

docs.title: Single-Variable Calculus
docs.text:
• Intuition and computation of limits;
  • Continuity, derivatives, differentials;
  • Mean value theorems, Taylor expansion;
  • Indefinite integrals, definite integrals, the fundamental theorem of calculus;
  • Simple differential equations, series.

docs.title: Linear Algebra
docs.text:
• Systems of linear equations and matrices;
  • Vector spaces, bases, dimension;
  • Linear maps, rank–nullity;
  • Eigenvalues, diagonalization;
  • Inner products, orthogonality, least squares.

docs.title: Multivariable Calculus
docs.text:
• Partial derivatives, gradients, total differentials;
  • Multiple integrals, change of variables;
  • Line and surface integrals;
  • Green, Gauss, and Stokes theorems.

docs.title: Discrete Mathematics and Proof
docs.text:
• Logic, sets, relations;
  • Induction and recursion;
  • Combinatorial counting;
  • Foundations of graph theory.

docs.title: Probability and Statistics
docs.text:
• Random variables, distributions, expectation, variance;
  • Laws of large numbers, central limit theorem (intuitive or proved, depending on the course);
  • Parameter estimation, hypothesis testing, regression.

docs.title: Mathematical Analysis and Real Analysis
docs.text:
A rigorous proof-based route is adopted: completeness of the real numbers, metric spaces, limits, continuity, differentiation, the Riemann integral, sequences of functions and uniform convergence, multivariable analysis. The Rudin System of analysis belongs here.

Difference from common calculus: common calculus emphasizes computation and application; analysis emphasizes definitions, proofs, and counterexamples.

docs.title: Abstract Algebra
docs.text: Groups, rings, fields, homomorphisms, quotient structures, group actions, field extensions. This requires experience with sets, mappings, equivalence relations, and linear algebra.

docs.title: Foundations of Geometry and Topology
docs.text: Metric spaces, topological spaces, continuous maps, compactness, connectedness, quotient spaces; an introduction to curves and surfaces.

docs.title: Differential Equations and Numerical Methods
docs.text: Existence and uniqueness for ordinary differential equations, linear systems, stability; numerical approximation, error, convergence.

docs.title: Advanced Topics
docs.text: Topic Prerequisites Measure Theory and the Lebesgue Integral Real analysis, sequences of functions, countable operations Complex Analysis Complex numbers, foundations of single-variable and multivariable analysis Functional Analysis Linear algebra, metric spaces, normed spaces Differential Geometry Multivariable calculus, linear algebra, foundations of topology Algebraic Topology Topology, group theory Algebraic Number Theory Rings, fields, field extensions Analytic Number Theory Number theory, real analysis, complex analysis Optimization Linear algebra, calculus, convex analysis Stochastic Processes Probability theory, foundations of analysis

docs.title: Suggested Study Routes
docs.text:
• Applied / engineering direction: common calculus + linear algebra + probability and statistics + differential equations / numerical methods;
  • Mathematics major: proceed directly to rigorous analysis + abstract algebra + topology, with the common computation courses serving as a supplement to intuition;
  • Analysis direction: real analysis → measure theory → functional / complex analysis;
  • Algebra / number theory direction: abstract algebra → field theory / commutative algebra → algebraic number theory;
  • Geometry / topology direction: topology → differential geometry / algebraic topology.

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
• Be able to explain the difference between the common calculus course and the analysis course.
  • Be able to list three prerequisites each for mathematical analysis, abstract algebra, and topology.
  • Be able to explain why linear algebra can be studied in parallel with calculus.

docs.title: Classical Academic System · Overview
docs.text: The Classical Academic System comprises two parallel routes: the Regular System and the Rudin System. The two routes share the same body of concepts but organize them differently: the Regular System proceeds by topic, whereas the Rudin System advances chapter by chapter along the lines of an analysis textbook.

docs.title: Two Systems
docs.text:
System Positioning Entry Regular System logic, sets, number systems, algebra, spaces, branches, advanced theory Start from logic Rudin System an analysis route built around Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis Chapter 1

The two systems do not replace each other: the Regular System supplies the common language and structures, whereas the Rudin System unfolds the analysis portion chapter by chapter.

docs.title: Regular System
docs.text:
Chapter Content Main prerequisites Logic, Language, and Proof propositions, predicates, quantifiers, proof methods none Sets, Relations, and Mappings set operations, relations, equivalence classes, mappings logic Natural Numbers and Number Systems Peano axioms, integers/rationals/reals, complex numbers logic, sets Algebraic Structures and Linear Spaces groups, rings, fields, vector spaces, linear maps sets, number systems Spaces, Limits, and Continuity metric spaces, open and closed sets, convergence, compactness, continuity number systems, algebra Core Branches analysis, algebra, number theory, geometry, topology, combinatorics, probability depends on the branch Advanced Theory measure theory, complex analysis, functional analysis, differential geometry, algebraic topology depends on the topic

There is no rule that the chapters must be taken in sequence; the table above is merely a recommended order. Branches may be pursued in parallel, provided that the prerequisites are complete.

docs.title: Rudin System
docs.text:
Chapter Content Status Chapter 1 · The Real and Complex Number Systems ordered fields, supremum, Archimedean property, n-th roots, complex numbers, Schwarz Expanded Chapter 2 · Basic Topology metric spaces, compactness, connectedness, Cantor set Expanded Chapter 3 · Sequences and Series convergence, Cauchy, limit superior and limit inferior, convergence tests for series Expanded Chapter 4 · Continuity limits of functions, continuity, uniform continuity, discontinuities Expanded Chapter 5 · Differentiation derivatives, mean value theorem, Taylor, L'Hôpital Expanded Chapter 6 · The Riemann–Stieltjes Integral partitions, integrability, integration by parts, rectifiable curves Expanded Chapter 7 · Sequences and Series of Functions uniform convergence, M-test, Arzelà–Ascoli Expanded Chapter 8 · Some Special Functions exponential, logarithm, trigonometric, Fourier, Gamma Expanded Chapter 9 · Functions of Several Variables derivatives, contraction mapping, inverse/implicit function Expanded Chapter 10 · Integration of Differential Forms differential forms, Stokes, Poincaré lemma Expanded Chapter 11 · The Lebesgue Theory measure, measurable functions, integration, L² Expanded

"Expanded" does not mean that every theorem has been proved in full; for the status of individual proofs see Proof Status and Core Proofs.

docs.title: Recommended Reading Order
docs.text:
1. Establish the language first: logic → sets → number systems.
  2. Then choose a structure: algebra → spaces; or proceed directly to Rudin Chapter 1.
  3. Analysis route: Rudin Chapters 1 → 2 → 3 → … → 11.
  4. Branch route: enter the analysis, algebra, number theory, geometry, topology, combinatorics, or probability material of Chapter 6 according to interest.
  5. Advanced study: enter the measure theory, complex analysis, functional analysis, geometry, and algebraic topology material of Chapter 7 according to topic.

docs.title: Page Conventions
docs.text:
As far as possible, every page should contain:

  • prerequisites;
  • definitions and core results;
  • proofs or an explicit proof status;
  • interfaces to adjacent chapters;
  • checkpoints or exercises.

This is an extensible knowledge map, not a verbatim copy of any textbook. The Rudin route is rewritten chapter by chapter; the Regular System is rewritten by topic.

docs.title: Logic, Language, and Proof
docs.text:
Source: Standard logic textbooks; Wikipedia: Propositional calculus, First-order logic.

Prerequisites: None. Goal of this chapter: First learn "how mathematical sentences are written, how they are negated, and how they are proved", then move on to concrete objects.

docs.title: 1.1 Propositions and Logical Connectives
docs.text:
A proposition is a declarative sentence with a definite truth value. Questions, imperatives, and sentences containing undetermined variables are not propositions in themselves.

Connective Symbol Reading When it is true Negation \( eg P\) not \(P\) when \(P\) is false Conjunction \(P \land Q\) \(P\) and \(Q\) both are true Disjunction \(P \lor Q\) \(P\) or \(Q\) at least one is true (the mathematical "or" usually includes the case where both are true) Implication \(P o Q\) if \(P\) then \(Q\) false only when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false Equivalence \(P \leftrightarrow Q\) \(P\) if and only if \(Q\) both have the same truth value

Common Pitfalls

  • \(P o Q\) does not mean "\(P\) is the cause of \(Q\)"; it expresses only a truth-value relation.
  • \(P o Q\) and \(Q o P\) are not equivalent; the former is the converse of the latter.
  • \( eg(P \land Q)\) is not \( eg P \land eg Q\), but \( eg P \lor eg Q\) (De Morgan).

docs.title: 1.2 Predicates and Quantifiers
docs.text:
A predicate is a statement containing variables, for example \(P(x)\): "\(x\) is even". Only after a range is assigned to the variable does it become a proposition.

Quantifier Symbol Reading Negation Universal \(\forall x \in S,\ P(x)\) for all \(x\) in \(S\), \(P(x)\) \(\exists x \in S,\ \neg P(x)\) Existential \(\exists x \in S,\ P(x)\) there exists \(x\) in \(S\) such that \(P(x)\) \(\forall x \in S,\ \neg P(x)\)

The order of quantifiers cannot be exchanged at will:

\[ \forall \varepsilon>0\ \exists N\ \forall n>N:\ |a_n-a|<\varepsilon \]

and

\[ \exists N\ \forall \varepsilon>0\ \forall n>N:\ |a_n-a|<\varepsilon \]

have completely different meanings. The former is "convergence"; the latter requires that "from some term onward all terms equal \(a\)".

Negation exercise: negate "for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(N\) such that for all \(n>N\), \(|a_n-a|<\varepsilon\)".

Answer: there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every \(N\) there exists \(n>N\) with \(|a_n-a|\ge \varepsilon\).

docs.title: 1.3 Definitions, Axioms, Theorems
docs.text:
Word Role Example Primitive notion not defined; only its use is stipulated set, membership Definition precisely specifies a new object by means of existing concepts "if \(f(x_1)=f(x_2)\) implies \(x_1=x_2\), we call \(f\) injective" Axiom an assumption serving as the starting point Peano axioms, axiom of choice Theorem a proposition derived from axioms, definitions, and proved results Pythagorean theorem, mean value theorem Lemma a small auxiliary result serving the proof of a main theorem Zorn's lemma Corollary a conclusion obtained directly from a theorem the monotonicity criterion derived from the mean value theorem

Definitions must be decidable: one cannot put "good", "natural", or "sufficiently large" into a definition without quantification.

docs.title: 1.4 Basic Proof Methods
docs.text:
Method Applicable situation Structure Direct proof to prove \(P o Q\) assume \(P\), derive \(Q\) Proof by contrapositive deriving \(Q\) directly is difficult prove \( eg Q o eg P\) Proof by contradiction assuming the conclusion false leads to a contradiction assume \( eg Q\), derive a contradiction Proof by cases the object splits according to cases prove that each case holds, and that the cases are exhaustive Existence proof to prove \(\exists x,\ P(x)\) construct an \(x\), or prove non-constructively that it cannot fail to exist Uniqueness proof to prove "there exists and is unique" first prove existence, then prove that any two objects satisfying the conditions are equal

Counterexample: to negate \( orall x,\ P(x)\), it suffices to give a single \(x\) with \( eg P(x)\). A counterexample must be concrete; it is not enough to say "it may fail".

docs.title: 1.5 Checking an Argument
docs.text:
After a proof has been written, check four things:

  1. Have the hypotheses been used? Does each hypothesis play a role in the proof;
  2. Is the scope correct? Are the variables in the correct sets;
  3. Is the direction of the equality/inequality correct? Does multiplying both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverse the sign;
  4. Is there any circularity? Is the conclusion used to prove the conclusion, or is a proposition equivalent to the conclusion used as a premise.

Mathematical induction is not developed systematically here, because it requires the structure of the natural numbers to be established first; see Number Systems.

docs.title: 1.6 Common Equivalences
docs.text:
Equivalence Name \( eg(P\land Q)\equiv eg P\lor eg Q\) De Morgan \( eg(P\lor Q)\equiv eg P\land eg Q\) De Morgan \(P o Q\equiv eg P\lor Q\) disjunctive form of implication \( eg(P o Q)\equiv P\land eg Q\) negation of implication \(P o Q\equiv eg Q o eg P\) contrapositive \( eg orall x\,P(x)\equiv\exists x\, eg P(x)\) quantifier negation \( eg\exists x\,P(x)\equiv orall x\, eg P(x)\) quantifier negation

Method for proving equivalences: construct a truth table; or perform algebraic manipulation using known equivalences. The truth table is a decision method for propositional logic, but its size grows exponentially with the number of variables.

docs.title: 1.7 Soundness and Completeness
docs.text:
Let "provable" be denoted \(\vdash\varphi\), and "true under all interpretations" be denoted \(\models\varphi\).

  • Soundness: if \(\vdash\varphi\), then \(\models\varphi\). The proof system does not derive false propositions.
  • Completeness: if \(\models\varphi\), then \(\vdash\varphi\). Every logically valid proposition can be proved.

Both propositional logic and first-order logic have soundness and completeness theorems; the completeness of first-order logic was proved by Gödel in 1929. Here we use only the distinction between "provable" and "valid", and do not develop the details of proof systems and model theory.

Proof status on this site: propositional equivalences and quantifier negation have complete proofs; soundness and completeness are deferred, since they require proof systems and model theory.

Note: completeness is not the same concept as "a theory is complete with respect to some model" (every sentence or its negation is provable); the latter belongs to the context of model theory/incompleteness theorems.

docs.title: 1.8 References
docs.text:
• Propositional calculus
  • First-order logic
  • Mathematical proof
  • Soundness
  • Completeness (logic)

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
• Be able to write the truth table for \(P \to Q\), and explain why "a false proposition implies any proposition" does not affect mathematical proofs.
  • Be able to correctly negate a proposition with two quantifiers.
  • Be able to distinguish "converse", "inverse", and "contrapositive".
  • Be able to give an example of something that "exists but is not unique", and explain what the uniqueness proof lacks.

docs.title: Sets, Relations, and Mappings
docs.text:
Sources: standard ZF/ZFC formulation; Wikipedia: Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory, Axiom of choice.

Prerequisite: logic (propositions, quantifiers, proofs). Goal of this chapter: to establish the object language shared by all subsequent branches of mathematics.

docs.title: 2.1 Sets and Membership
docs.text:
A set is a totality of objects; \(x \in A\) means that \(x\) is an element of \(A\), while \(x \notin A\) means that it is not.

  • Axiom of extensionality: two sets are equal if and only if they have the same elements.
  • Subset: \(A \subseteq B\) means \(\forall x,\ x\in A \to x\in B\).
  • Proper subset: \(A \subsetneq B\) means \(A\subseteq B\) and \(A\ne B\).

The empty set \(\varnothing\) is the unique set with no elements. Note that both \(\varnothing \in \{\varnothing\}\) and \(\varnothing \subseteq \{\varnothing\}\) hold, but they mean different things.

docs.title: 2.2 Basic Set Operations
docs.text:
Operation Definition Remark Intersection \(A\cap B=\{x:x\in A\land x\in B\}\) the intersection may be empty Union \(A\cup B=\{x:x\in A\lor x\in B\}\) "or" includes both Difference \(A\setminus B=\{x:x\in A\land x\notin B\}\) \(B\subseteq A\) is not required Complement \(A^c=\{x\in U:x\notin A\}\) the universal set \(U\) must be specified first Power set \(\mathcal P(A)=\{B:B\subseteq A\}\) if \(\lvert A\rvert=n\), then \(\lvert\mathcal P(A)\rvert=2^n\)

De Morgan:

\[ (A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c,\qquad (A\cap B)^c=A^c\cup B^c. \]

docs.title: 2.3 Introduction to Axiomatic Set Theory
docs.text:
Using "the set of all sets" without restriction leads to a paradox (Russell's paradox). Axiomatic set theory restricts the construction of sets by means of the axiom schema of separation:

\[ \{x\in A:\ P(x)\} \]

One must first have a set \(A\) and then select from it; one cannot write \(\{x:\ P(x)\}\) without specifying where \(x\) comes from.

The axioms commonly used include: empty set, pairing, union, power set, infinity, replacement, and choice. Here it suffices to know that "sets cannot collect objects arbitrarily"; the full axiomatization is deferred to a later treatment of set theory.

docs.title: 2.4 Ordered Pairs and Cartesian Products
docs.text:
The essential feature of an ordered pair \((a,b)\) is order: \((a,b)=(c,d)\) if and only if \(a=c\) and \(b=d\).

Cartesian product:

\[ A\times B=\{(a,b):a\in A,\ b\in B\}. \]

In general, \(A_1\times\cdots\times A_n\) denotes the set of \(n\)-tuples.

docs.title: 2.5 Binary Relations
docs.text:
A binary relation from \(A\) to \(B\) is a subset of \(A\times B\). If \(R\subseteq A\times A\), we call \(R\) a relation on \(A\).

Property Definition Reflexive \(\forall x\in A,\ (x,x)\in R\) Symmetric \((x,y)\in R \to (y,x)\in R\) Transitive \((x,y),(y,z)\in R \to (x,z)\in R\) Antisymmetric \((x,y),(y,x)\in R \to x=y\)

An equivalence relation = reflexive + symmetric + transitive. It partitions the set into pairwise disjoint equivalence classes:

\[ [x]=\{y\in A:(x,y)\in R\}. \]

A partition is a family of pairwise disjoint subsets of \(A\) whose union is \(A\). Equivalence relations and partitions are in one-to-one correspondence.

An order relation usually means a partial order (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive); a total order additionally requires that any two elements be comparable.

docs.title: 2.6 Mappings
docs.text:
A mapping \(f:A\to B\) assigns to each \(x\in A\) a unique \(f(x)\in B\).

  • Domain \(A\), codomain \(B\);
  • Image \(f(A)=\{f(x):x\in A\}\);
  • Preimage \(f^{-1}(S)=\{x\in A:f(x)\in S\}\).
Property Definition Negation Injective \(f(x_1)=f(x_2)\to x_1=x_2\) there exist \(x_1\ne x_2\) with \(f(x_1)=f(x_2)\) Surjective \(\forall y\in B,\ \exists x\in A,\ f(x)=y\) there exists \(y\in B\) not in the image Bijective both injective and surjective there is a collision or a missed value

Note: surjectivity is relative to the codomain; changing the codomain changes surjectivity.

docs.title: 2.7 Operations on Mappings
docs.text:
• Composition: \((g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))\), which requires the codomain of \(f\) to be compatible with the domain of \(g\).
  • Inverse mapping: if \(f:A\to B\) is bijective, then there exists \(f^{-1}:B\to A\) satisfying \(f^{-1}(f(x))=x\) and \(f(f^{-1}(y))=y\).
  • Restriction: restricting the domain of \(f\) to a subset \(S\subseteq A\), written \(f|_S\).

Composition is in general not commutative: \(f\circ g\ne g\circ f\), and indeed both sides need not even be defined.

docs.title: 2.8 Families of Sets and Quotient Sets
docs.text:
A family of sets \(\{A_i\}_{i\in I}\) is a family of sets indexed by an index set \(I\); one may form the union \(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\) and the intersection \(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i\).

The quotient set \(A/{\sim}\) is the set whose elements are the equivalence classes:

\[ A/{\sim}=\{[x]:x\in A\}. \]

The quotient set is the formal language for "identifying objects according to an equivalence relation". The integers, the rational numbers, quotient groups, and quotient rings are all constructed by means of it.

docs.title: Dependency Rules
docs.text:
• Equivalence relations must precede quotient sets;
  • Mappings must precede isomorphisms;
  • Order relations must precede supremum/infimum;
  • Power sets and Cartesian products must precede relations and function spaces.

docs.title: 2.9 The Axiom of Choice and Zorn's Lemma
docs.text:
Axiom of Choice (AC): for any family of sets \(\{A_i\}_{i\in I}\) consisting of non-empty sets, there exists a choice function \(f\) such that \(f(i)\in A_i\) holds for every \(i\).

Equivalent forms:

  • Zorn's lemma: if every chain in a non-empty partially ordered set \(P\) has an upper bound, then \(P\) has a maximal element;
  • Well-ordering theorem: every set can be well-ordered;
  • Tychonoff's theorem (topology): the product of arbitrary compact spaces is compact.

Zorn's lemma is commonly used in existence proofs for "maximal ideals", "Hamel bases", "algebraic closures", and the like. It does not construct the object; it only guarantees that a maximal object exists. The chain of equivalences among AC, Zorn's lemma, and the well-ordering theorem is deferred for proof (it requires axiomatic set theory).

Boundary: AC differs from "finite choice"; the selection of finitely many non-empty sets does not require AC. The difference between ZF and ZFC lies precisely in whether AC is adjoined.

docs.title: 2.10 The Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein Theorem
docs.text:
If there exist an injection \(f:A\to B\) and an injection \(g:B\to A\), then there exists a bijection \(h:A\to B\).

Consequently, "\(|A|\le|B|\) and \(|B|\le|A|\)" implies "\(|A|=|B|\)". This theorem does not depend on AC; it shows that the comparison of cardinalities can be defined by means of injections.

Complete proof: define the bijection piecewise using \(C_0=A\setminus g(B)\), \(C_{n+1}=g(f(C_n))\), and \(C=\bigcup C_n\); see proofs page §4.

Cantor's theorem: there is no surjection from \(A\) onto \(\mathcal P(A)\), hence \(|A|<|\mathcal P(A)|\); for the complete proof see proofs page §3.

docs.title: 2.11 References
docs.text:
• Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory
  • Axiom of choice
  • Zorn's lemma
  • Schröder–Bernstein theorem
  • Equivalence relation

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
• Be able to prove "equivalence relation ↔ partition".
  • Be able to determine whether a mapping is injective/surjective, and to write down the negation.
  • Be able to explain why \(\{x:P(x)\}\) cannot be used unconditionally.
  • Be able to explain the difference between a quotient set and "choosing a representative".

docs.title: Natural Numbers and the Construction of Number Systems
docs.text:
Sources: Rudin, Chapter 1; Peano axioms, Dedekind cut.

Prerequisite: logic and sets (proofs, sets, equivalence relations, mappings). Goal of this chapter: not merely to "recognize the various kinds of numbers", but to explain how they are obtained and why their operations are valid.

docs.title: 3.1 Natural Numbers
docs.text:
The natural numbers can be characterized by the Peano axioms (starting from an initial object and a successor operation):

  1. \(0\in\mathbb N\);
  2. there exists a successor mapping \(S:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\);
  3. \(S(n)\ne 0\) for all \(n\);
  4. \(S\) is injective;
  5. if \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\) contains \(0\), and \(n\in A\to S(n)\in A\), then \(A=\mathbb N\).

Axiom 5 is precisely the principle of induction. It allows a proof that a statement holds "for all natural numbers" to be divided into two steps: the base case and the inductive step.

Recursive definition: if the new value at each step depends only on the preceding step (or on finitely many preceding steps), then a function may be defined recursively on \(\mathbb N\). For example, the factorial:

\[ 0!=1,\qquad (n+1)!=(n+1)\cdot n!. \]

docs.title: 3.2 Operations on Natural Numbers and Divisibility
docs.text:
• Addition: \(m+0=m\), \(m+S(n)=S(m+n)\);
  • Multiplication: \(m\cdot 0=0\), \(m\cdot S(n)=m\cdot n+m\);
  • Order: \(a\le b\) if and only if there exists \(k\) such that \(a+k=b\).

Division algorithm: for \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b>0\), there exist unique \(q,r\) such that

\[ a=bq+r,\qquad 0\le r<b. \]

Prime: a natural number greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. Fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every natural number greater than 1 admits a unique factorization into a product of primes (order disregarded).

docs.title: 3.3 The Integers
docs.text:
The integers may be regarded as equivalence classes of pairs of natural numbers:

\[ (a,b)\sim(c,d)\iff a+d=b+c. \]

Intuitively, \((a,b)\) represents \(a-b\). Addition and multiplication are defined by

\[ [(a,b)]+[(c,d)]=[(a+c,b+d)], \] \[ [(a,b)]\cdot[(c,d)]=[(ac+bd,\ ad+bc)]. \]

One must verify that these definitions are independent of the choice of representatives (well-defined). The integers make subtraction closed.

docs.title: 3.4 The Rational Numbers
docs.text:
The rational numbers may be regarded as equivalence classes of pairs of integers:

\[ (a,b)\sim(c,d)\iff ad=bc,\qquad b,d\ne 0. \]

\((a,b)\) represents \(a/b\). Addition, multiplication, and order are induced by the operations on the integers; one must exclude the zero denominator and verify well-definedness. The rational numbers make division (by non-zero numbers) closed, and they are dense: between any two rational numbers there lies another rational number.

docs.title: 3.5 The Real Numbers and Dedekind Cuts
docs.text:
Although the rational numbers are dense, they are not complete: for example, \(\sqrt2\) is not rational. One way to construct the real numbers is the Dedekind cut.

A set \(A\subseteq\mathbb Q\) is called a cut if:

  1. \(A\ne\varnothing\) and \(A\ne\mathbb Q\);
  2. if \(a\in A\) and \(b<a\), then \(b\in A\) (closed downward);
  3. \(A\) has no greatest element.

Each cut represents a real number; the rational number \(q\) corresponds to the cut \(\{x\in\mathbb Q:x<q\}\). The operations and the order on the real numbers are defined by inclusion, union, translation, and the like on cuts.

Completeness (least-upper-bound property): every non-empty subset of the real numbers that is bounded above has a supremum. This is the foundation of the results of analysis concerning limits, continuity, compactness, and the like.

One may also construct the real numbers by means of Cauchy sequences; this requires the language of limits and metrics first, and is therefore placed later as "another construction". The advantage of the Dedekind cut is that it does not depend on the theory of limits.

docs.title: 3.6 The Complex Numbers
docs.text:
The complex numbers may be regarded as pairs of real numbers \((a,b)\), with the definitions

\[ (a,b)+(c,d)=(a+c,b+d), \] \[ (a,b)\cdot(c,d)=(ac-bd,\ ad+bc). \]

Writing \(i=(0,1)\), we have \((a,b)=a+bi\) and \(i^2=-1\). The field of complex numbers is algebraically closed: every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has a root (the fundamental theorem of algebra).

docs.title: 3.7 Finite, Countable, and Uncountable Sets
docs.text:
• Sets \(A\) and \(B\) are equinumerous if there exists a bijection \(A\to B\);
  • Finite: equinumerous with some \(\{1,\dots,n\}\);
  • Countably infinite: equinumerous with \(\mathbb N\);
  • Uncountable: neither finite nor countably infinite.

Cantor's theorem: \(|A|<|\mathcal P(A)|\), hence \(\mathbb R\) is uncountable. Finite unions and countable unions of countable sets remain countable; \(\mathbb Q\) is countable and \(\mathbb R\) is uncountable.

docs.title: Dependency Rules
docs.text:
• The natural numbers must precede induction;
  • The integers/rational numbers must follow equivalence classes and quotient sets;
  • Completeness of the reals must precede the theory of limits;
  • The complex numbers must follow the arithmetic of the reals;
  • Comparison of cardinalities must follow bijections.

docs.title: 3.8 Equivalent Forms of Completeness of the Real Numbers
docs.text:
In the ordered field \(\mathbb R\), the following properties are equivalent (under the assumption that the Archimedean property holds):

  1. Supremum property: every non-empty subset that is bounded above has a supremum;
  2. Monotone convergence: every bounded monotone sequence converges;
  3. Nested intervals: the intersection of a nested sequence of closed intervals is non-empty (when the lengths tend to 0, the intersection is a single point);
  4. Bolzano–Weierstrass: every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence;
