  5. Cauchy completeness: every Cauchy sequence converges.

Different textbooks start from different properties and then derive the others as theorems. This site constructs \(\mathbb R\) from Dedekind cuts, and therefore takes the supremum property as the first completeness theorem following the definition; for the complete proof of the supremum property see proofs page §6. The remaining equivalent forms are deferred for proof.

Archimedean property: for every \(x\in\mathbb R\) there exists \(n\in\mathbb N\) such that \(n>x\). It guarantees that \(\mathbb N\) is unbounded in \(\mathbb R\), and it is also the foundation of "\(\frac1n\to0\)".

docs.title: 3.9 The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
docs.text:
Every polynomial of degree \(n\ge1\) with complex coefficients

\[ p(z)=a_nz^n+\cdots+a_1z+a_0,\qquad a_n\ne0 \]

has at least one root in \(\mathbb C\); hence it factors as

\[ p(z)=a_n\prod_{k=1}^n(z-z_k) \]

(multiplicities counted). This shows that \(\mathbb C\) is algebraically closed; but \(\mathbb R\) is not (\(x^2+1\) has no real root).

The proof may be given by complex analysis (Liouville's theorem) or by algebraic topology (winding number); this site treats it as a conclusion concerning "properties of the field of complex numbers" and defers the proof, which is placed in the complex analysis branch.

docs.title: 3.10 Cardinality and the Continuum
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb Q\) is countable: one may enumerate by the height of the numerator and denominator;
  • \(\mathbb R\) is uncountable: Cantor's diagonal argument;
  • \(|\mathbb R|=|\mathcal P(\mathbb N)|=2^{\aleph_0}\);
  • Continuum hypothesis (CH): \(2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1\). CH is independent of ZFC: it can be neither proved nor refuted (Gödel 1938, Cohen 1963).

Note: uncountable does not mean "one more than \(\mathbb N\)"; the comparison of cardinalities is defined by means of bijections/injections.

docs.title: 3.11 References
docs.text:
• Peano axioms
  • Dedekind cut
  • Construction of the real numbers
  • Completeness of the real numbers
  • Fundamental theorem of algebra
  • Continuum hypothesis

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
• Be able to write down the Peano axioms and explain why induction is valid.
  • Be able to construct the integers or the rational numbers by means of equivalence classes, and verify that the operations are well-defined.
  • Be able to explain how a Dedekind cut expresses \(\sqrt2\).
  • Be able to prove that \(\mathbb Q\) is countable and \(\mathbb R\) is uncountable (at least state the idea of the diagonal argument).

docs.title: Algebraic Structures and Linear Spaces
docs.text:
Source: Standard abstract algebra textbooks; Wikipedia: Group, Ring, Field, Vector space.

Prerequisites: Sets and number systems (sets, mappings, equivalence relations, number systems). Goal of this chapter: To abstract the common structures from concrete number systems and to establish the language of linear algebra.

docs.title: 4.1 Operations and Algebraic Structures
docs.text:
A binary operation on a set \(A\) is a mapping \(A\times A\to A\). It must assign a unique result to every ordered pair, and the result must again lie in \(A\) (closure).

An algebraic structure = a set + several operations + the axioms satisfied by these operations.

docs.title: 4.2 Groups
docs.text:
A group \((G,\cdot)\) satisfies:

  1. Associativity: \((ab)c=a(bc)\);
  2. Identity element: there exists \(e\in G\) such that \(ea=ae=a\);
  3. Inverse element: for every \(a\in G\) there exists \(a^{-1}\) such that \(aa^{-1}=a^{-1}a=e\).

If in addition the commutative law \(ab=ba\) holds, the group is called an abelian group.

Examples: \((\mathbb Z,+)\), \((\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\},\cdot)\), \(GL_n(\mathbb R)\) (invertible matrices under multiplication), and the permutation group \(S_n\).

Subgroup: a non-empty subset \(H\subseteq G\) that is closed under multiplication and inverses. Lagrange's theorem: in a finite group, the order of a subgroup divides the order of the group.

docs.title: 4.3 Rings and Fields
docs.text:
A ring \((R,+,\cdot)\) satisfies: \((R,+)\) is an abelian group; multiplication is associative; multiplication distributes over addition.

  • Commutative ring: multiplication is commutative;
  • Ring with unity: there exists a multiplicative identity \(1\);
  • Integral domain: commutative, with unity, and without zero divisors (\(ab=0\to a=0\) or \(b=0\)).

A field is a commutative ring with unity in which every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse. Examples: \(\mathbb Q,\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb F_p\) (with \(p\) prime).

docs.title: 4.4 Homomorphisms and Isomorphisms
docs.text:
A mapping that preserves the operations is called a homomorphism:

  • Group homomorphism: \(\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)\);
  • Ring homomorphism: \(\varphi(a+b)=\varphi(a)+\varphi(b)\), \(\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)\).

A bijective homomorphism is called an isomorphism. Two structures related by an isomorphism are "the same" algebraically; only the names of the elements differ.

Kernel: \(\ker\varphi=\{g:\varphi(g)=e\}\). Fundamental theorem of group homomorphisms: \(G/\ker\varphi\cong \operatorname{im}\varphi\).

docs.title: 4.5 Vector Spaces
docs.text:
Let \(F\) be a field. A vector space \(V\) is an abelian group equipped with a scalar multiplication \(F\times V\to V\) satisfying:

\[ 1v=v,\qquad a(bv)=(ab)v, \] \[ a(u+v)=au+av,\qquad (a+b)v=av+bv. \]

The elements are called vectors, and \(F\) is called the base field. \(\mathbb R^n\) is the most typical example.

docs.title: 4.6 Bases, Dimension, and Linear Maps
docs.text:
• Linear combination: \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i\);
  • Span: every vector in \(V\) can be written as a finite linear combination;
  • Linear independence: if \(\sum a_i v_i=0\), then all \(a_i=0\);
  • Basis: linearly independent and spanning \(V\).

If \(V\) has a basis consisting of \(n\) vectors, then every basis consists of \(n\) vectors, and \(n\) is called the dimension.

A linear map \(T:V\to W\) satisfies \(T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)\). A linear map is uniquely determined by its values on a basis.

docs.title: 4.7 Matrices and Systems of Linear Equations
docs.text:
Once a basis is chosen, a linear map is represented by a matrix; composition corresponds to matrix multiplication. The solution set of the system \(Ax=b\):

  • The solution space of the homogeneous system \(Ax=0\) is the kernel;
  • If the inhomogeneous system is consistent, its solution set is an affine subspace (a particular solution plus the homogeneous solutions).

Rank–nullity theorem:

\[ \dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T. \]

docs.title: 4.8 Determinants, Eigenvalues, and Inner Products
docs.text:
• Determinant: an alternating multilinear function satisfying \(\det(AB)=\det A\det B\); \(\det A\ne0\) if and only if \(A\) is invertible.
  • Eigenvalue/eigenvector: \(Av=\lambda v\), \(v\ne0\). Characteristic polynomial \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\).
  • Inner product: positive definite, symmetric/conjugate symmetric, linear in the first argument; it induces the norm \(\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}\).
  • Orthogonality: \(\langle u,v\rangle=0\); an orthogonal basis simplifies coordinate computations.

docs.title: Dependencies and Boundaries
docs.text:
This chapter treats only the basic definitions and typical examples. Complete group theory (Sylow theorems, solvable groups), commutative algebra (ideals, localization), and field extensions (Galois theory) belong to the algebra branch of the Core Branches.

Before entering analysis, what is required is: the real and complex fields, vector spaces, inner products, norms, linear maps, and matrices; it is not necessary to have studied a complete course in advanced algebra first.

docs.title: 4.9 Fundamental Theorem of Group Homomorphisms
docs.text:
Let \(\varphi:G\to H\) be a group homomorphism. Then \(\ker\varphi\) is a normal subgroup of \(G\), and

\[ G/\ker\varphi\cong\operatorname{im}\varphi. \]

The isomorphism is given by \(g\ker\varphi\mapsto\varphi(g)\). This theorem converts "the image of a homomorphism" into "a quotient group" and is one of the earliest structure theorems in group theory; the complete proof is given in proofs page §8.

Corollary: \(\varphi\) is injective \(\iff \ker\varphi=\{e\}\).

docs.title: 4.10 Rank–Nullity Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(V,W\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field \(F\), and let \(T:V\to W\) be linear. Then

\[ \dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T. \]

Equivalently, \(\operatorname{rank}T+\operatorname{nullity}T=\dim V\). It states that the sum of the "dimensions lost" and the "dimensions retained" by a linear map equals the dimension of the domain; the complete proof is given in proofs page §9.

Corollary: if \(\dim V=\dim W\), then \(T\) is injective \(\iff\) surjective \(\iff\) invertible.

docs.title: 4.11 Spectral Theorem for Real Symmetric Matrices
docs.text:
If \(A\) is a real symmetric matrix (\(A=A^{\mathsf T}\)), then:

  1. All eigenvalues of \(A\) are real;
  2. Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal;
  3. There exists an orthogonal matrix \(Q\) such that \(A=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}\), where \(\Lambda\) is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the eigenvalues.

That is to say, a real symmetric matrix has a set of orthonormal eigenvectors forming a basis of \(\mathbb R^n\). Complex Hermitian matrices admit an analogous unitary diagonalization. This site defers the proof for now (it requires inner product spaces and induction).

docs.title: 4.12 References
docs.text:
• Group (mathematics)
  • Ring (mathematics)
  • Field (mathematics)
  • Vector space
  • Rank–nullity theorem
  • Spectral theorem
  • Isomorphism theorem

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
• Be able to verify whether a set together with a given operation forms a group/ring/field.
  • Be able to distinguish homomorphisms, isomorphisms, and automorphisms.
  • Be able to prove that the number of vectors in a basis does not depend on the choice of basis (finite-dimensional case).
  • Be able to state the rank–nullity theorem and use it to determine the structure of the solution set of a linear system.

docs.title: Spaces, Limits, and Continuity
docs.text:
Sources: Rudin, Chapter 2; Munkres, Topology; Wikipedia: Metric space, Compact space.

Prerequisite: number systems and algebra (real numbers, vector spaces, inner products, linear maps). Goal of this chapter: to turn "distance, closeness, continuity" from intuition into a language that admits proof. Rudin's system of analysis enters at this point.

docs.title: 5.1 Euclidean Spaces, Norms, and Distance
docs.text:
The Euclidean norm on \(\mathbb R^n\):

\[ \|x\|_2=\sqrt{x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2}. \]

The distance is \(d(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2\). More generally, a norm on a vector space satisfies:

  1. \(\|x\|\ge0\), and \(\|x\|=0\iff x=0\);
  2. \(\|\alpha x\|=|\alpha|\|x\|\);
  3. \(\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|\).

A norm induces the distance \(d(x,y)=\|x-y\|\). A distance satisfies positive definiteness, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.

docs.title: 5.2 Metric Spaces
docs.text:
A set \(X\) equipped with a distance \(d:X\times X\to[0,\infty)\) satisfying:

\[ d(x,y)=0\iff x=y,\qquad d(x,y)=d(y,x),\qquad d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z). \]

Examples: \(\mathbb R^n\), the discrete metric, the supremum metric on function spaces, and the \(L^1\) metric on \(C[0,1]\).

Open ball:

\[ B(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}. \]

docs.title: 5.3 Open Sets, Closed Sets, Neighborhoods, and Limit Points
docs.text:
• \(U\) is an open set: \(\forall x\in U,\ \exists r>0,\ B(x,r)\subseteq U\);
  • \(F\) is a closed set: \(X\setminus F\) is open;
  • Neighborhood: a set that contains some open ball and contains \(x\);
  • Limit point: every neighborhood of \(x\) contains a point of \(A\) distinct from \(x\);
  • Closure \(\overline A\): the union of \(A\) and all its limit points.

Key equivalence: \(F\) is closed \(\iff\) the limit of every convergent sequence in \(F\) still lies in \(F\) (metric spaces).

docs.title: 5.4 Sequences, Convergence, and Completeness
docs.text:
\(x_n\to x\) is defined by:

\[ \forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists N,\ \forall n>N:\ d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon. \]

Cauchy sequence:

\[ \forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists N,\ \forall m,n>N:\ d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon. \]

A convergent sequence is necessarily a Cauchy sequence; the converse need not hold. In a complete metric space every Cauchy sequence converges. \(\mathbb R^n\) is complete; \(\mathbb Q\) is not complete.

docs.title: 5.5 Compactness and Connectedness
docs.text:
• Compact: every open cover has a finite subcover. In a metric space this is equivalent to "every sequence has a convergent subsequence" (sequential compactness).
  • Heine–Borel: a subset of \(\mathbb R^n\) is compact \(\iff\) it is bounded and closed.
  • Connected: it cannot be written as the union of two non-empty disjoint open sets; the connected subsets of \(\mathbb R\) are the intervals.
  • Properties of continuous functions on compact sets: boundedness, attainment of maximum and minimum, uniform continuity.

docs.title: 5.6 Limits of Functions and Continuous Mappings
docs.text:
\(f:X\to Y\) is continuous at \(x_0\):

\[ \forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists\delta>0,\ d_X(x,x_0)<\delta\to d_Y(f(x),f(x_0))<\varepsilon. \]

Equivalent characterizations: the preimage of an open set is open; \(x_n\to x_0\) implies \(f(x_n)\to f(x_0)\).

Uniform continuity: \(\delta\) does not depend on \(x_0\). A continuous function on a compact set is uniformly continuous.

docs.title: 5.7 General Topological Spaces
docs.text:
Take "open set" as the primitive structure: a topology \(\tau\subseteq\mathcal P(X)\) is required to contain \(\varnothing,X\), and to be closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. Metric spaces are a special case of topological spaces.

General topology can branch off from this point as an independent route; classical calculus requires only the foundations of metric spaces, and one need not first study general topology in its entirety.

docs.title: Where the Rudin Analysis Route Belongs
docs.text:
Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis begins with the real number system and the language of topological/metric spaces, then proceeds to sequences and series, continuity, differentiation, integration, sequences of functions and uniform convergence, and multivariable analysis. The correspondence with this system is:

  1. number systems: completeness of the real numbers;
  2. spaces: metric spaces and continuity;
  3. branches: the analysis branch (series → differentiation/integration → sequences of functions → multivariable).

A complete course in abstract algebra is not required first, but norms, inner products, and linear maps from linear algebra are required.

docs.title: 5.8 Equivalent Characterizations of Completeness
docs.text:
In a metric space \((X,d)\):

  • \(X\) is complete \(\iff\) every Cauchy sequence converges;
  • \(X\) is complete \(\iff\) every absolutely convergent series converges (in the context of normed spaces);
  • in \(\mathbb R^n\), complete \(\iff\) every bounded closed set is complete;
  • Contraction mapping principle (Banach): if \(T:X\to X\) satisfies \(d(Tx,Ty)\le qd(x,y)\) (\(0\le q<1\)) and \(X\) is complete, then \(T\) has a unique fixed point; for the complete proof see proofs page §15.

The contraction mapping principle is a common tool for the existence and uniqueness of ordinary differential equations and for the convergence of numerical iterations.

docs.title: 5.9 Compactness: Heine–Borel and Bolzano–Weierstrass
docs.text:
Heine–Borel (\(\mathbb R^n\)): a subset \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is compact \(\iff\) \(K\) is bounded and closed. This site defers the proof (it requires real analysis).

Bolzano–Weierstrass: every bounded sequence in \(\mathbb R^n\) has a convergent subsequence.

In a metric space:

\[ \text{compact}\iff\text{sequentially compact}\iff\text{complete and totally bounded}. \]

Note: in a general topological space, compactness, sequential compactness, and limit point compactness need not be equivalent; conditions such as first countability or metrizability are required.

docs.title: 5.10 Continuous Functions on Compact and Connected Sets
docs.text:
• a continuous mapping carries compact sets to compact sets;
  • a continuous mapping carries connected sets to connected sets;
  • a real-valued continuous function on a non-empty compact set is bounded and attains its maximum and minimum (extreme value theorem); for the complete proof see proofs page §12–13.
  • a continuous function on a compact set is uniformly continuous;
  • the intermediate value theorem for continuous functions on \(\mathbb R\): if \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(f(a)<c<f(b)\), then there exists \(\xi\in(a,b)\) such that \(f(\xi)=c\).

These conclusions are a common source of "existence" proofs in analysis: first prove compactness/connectedness, then take an extremum or apply the intermediate value theorem. For the proof of the open-preimage characterization of continuity and of the continuous image of a compact set, see proofs page §11–12.

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
• Be able to prove that a union of open balls is open and that the complement of a closed set is open.
  • Be able to distinguish convergence, the Cauchy property, and completeness.
  • Be able to explain why a continuous function on a compact set attains its maximum.
  • Be able to write down the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition of a continuous mapping and the open-preimage characterization, and to prove that they are equivalent.

docs.title: Core Branches
docs.text:
Sources: standard textbooks and Wikipedia entries on analysis, algebra, number theory, geometry, topology, combinatorics, and probability.

Prerequisite: the corresponding parts of logic, sets, number systems, algebra, and spaces. The branches may be pursued in parallel, but each branch uses only the prerequisites listed for it.

This page is not a queue in which one subject must be finished before the next is begun, but a map on which one chooses an entry point within a shared language.

docs.title: Overview of the Branches
docs.text: Branch Suggested internal order Required background Not required Analysis Series of numbers → single-variable differentiation and integration → sequences of functions and uniform convergence → multivariable calculus real numbers, metric spaces; linear algebra for the multivariable part abstract algebra is not required beforehand Algebra Group theory → quotient groups; ring theory → ideals and quotient rings; field theory → field extensions basic algebraic structures, equivalence relations, mappings analysis is not required beforehand Number Theory Divisibility and congruences → arithmetic functions → deeper problems on integers natural numbers, integers, induction; groups and rings in part the elementary part does not require analysis Geometry Axioms and proofs of Euclidean geometry → analytic geometry → curves and surfaces basic logic; linear algebra for analytic geometry; calculus for curves and surfaces topology is not required beforehand Topology General topology → product and quotient spaces → deeper topological properties sets, mappings, basic notions of space algebraic topology is not required beforehand Combinatorics Counting principles → combinatorial identities → recurrences and graph theory natural numbers, sets, mappings, induction analysis is not required Probability Theory Finite probability spaces → conditional probability and independence → discrete random variables sets, counting, real numbers; series for the infinite discrete case axiomatic probability theory is deferred to Advanced Theory

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
Entry point: completeness of the real numbers + metric spaces + continuity.

  1. Series of numbers: partial sums, convergence tests, absolute convergence, power series;
  2. Single-variable differentiation: derivative, mean value theorem, Taylor expansion, extrema;
  3. Single-variable integration: Riemann integral, fundamental theorem of calculus, substitution and integration by parts;
  4. Sequences of functions and uniform convergence: pointwise vs uniform, interchange of limits, Weierstrass test;
  5. Multivariable calculus: partial derivatives, total differential, multiple integrals, line/surface integrals, theorems of Stokes type.

Boundary: measure theory and the Lebesgue integral (Advanced Theory) are entered only after the Riemann integral; when only the Riemann integral has been studied, one must not treat "integrable" as a measure-theoretic conclusion.

docs.title: Algebra
docs.text:
Entry point: the basic definitions of groups, rings, and fields + homomorphisms.

  1. Group theory: subgroups, cosets, normal subgroups, quotient groups, fundamental theorem on homomorphisms, group actions;
  2. Ring theory: ideals, quotient rings, integral domains, unique factorization domains, polynomial rings;
  3. Field theory: field extensions, algebraic extensions, splitting fields, Galois theory (advanced).

Boundary: linear algebra is not abstract algebra; matrix computation may be completed within algebra, while the structure theory of groups, rings, and fields is developed here.

docs.title: Number Theory
docs.text:
Entry point: divisibility, Euclidean algorithm, fundamental theorem of arithmetic.

  1. Elementary number theory: congruences, linear congruences, CRT, Fermat/Euler theorems, primitive roots;
  2. Arithmetic functions: \(\varphi,\mu,\tau,\sigma\) and Dirichlet convolution;
  3. Advanced topics: quadratic residues, quadratic reciprocity, Diophantine equations, analytic/algebraic number theory (Advanced Theory).

Boundary: elementary number theory may begin at the secondary-school competition stage; analytic number theory requires complex analysis.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
Entry point: the axioms and proofs of Euclidean geometry; analytic geometry uses linear algebra.

  1. Euclidean geometry: axioms, congruence, similarity, circles, straightedge-and-compass constructions;
  2. Analytic geometry: coordinates, lines/circles, conic sections, vector methods;
  3. Curves and surfaces: parametrization, curvature, first/second fundamental forms (calculus).

Boundary: differential geometry requires multivariable calculus and linear algebra; algebraic topology requires topology and group theory.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
Entry point: sets, mappings, open sets and continuity in metric spaces.

  1. General topology: topological spaces, bases, subspaces, continuity, compactness, connectedness, separation axioms;
  2. Product and quotient spaces: product topology, quotient topology, adjunction spaces;
  3. Further topics: compactification, metrization, fundamental group (algebraic topology, Advanced Theory).

docs.title: Combinatorics
docs.text:
Entry point: natural numbers, sets, mappings, induction.

  1. Counting principles: addition/multiplication principles, permutations and combinations, binomial theorem;
  2. Combinatorial identities: double counting, generating functions, inclusion–exclusion;
  3. Recurrences and graph theory: recurrence relations, generating functions, basic notions of graphs, trees, matchings.

docs.title: Probability Theory
docs.text:
Entry point: sets, counting, real numbers; series for the infinite discrete case.

  1. Finite probability spaces: sample space, events, axioms of probability (finite version);
  2. Conditional probability and independence: Bayes, total probability, independent repeated trials;
  3. Discrete random variables: distributions, expectation, variance, common distributions;
  4. Limit theorems: laws of large numbers, central limit theorem (requires a background in analysis/measure theory).

Boundary: axiomatic probability theory (probability on measure spaces) belongs to Advanced Theory; undefined notions such as "almost surely" must not be used within a branch.

docs.title: Quick Reference of Core Theorems
docs.text:

The proofs of these theorems are dispersed across the corresponding branches; this page provides only the "name—prerequisite—location". Apart from the entries already proved in full on the proofs page, all the others are deferred for proof, and must not be cited directly on pages that lack the prerequisites.

docs.title: Suggestions on the Order of Choice
docs.text:
• To fill in rigorous analysis: number systems, real numbers → spaces, metric spaces → the analysis branch;
  • To fill in algebra: sets, equivalence relations → algebra, groups/rings/fields → the algebra branch;
  • To fill in geometry/topology: algebra, linear algebra → spaces, spaces → geometry/topology;
  • To fill in number theory/combinatorics: number systems, natural numbers/induction → number theory or combinatorics;
  • To fill in probability: sets/counting + real numbers → probability; for the continuous case, add integration later.

docs.title: Advanced Theory and Interdisciplinary Fields
docs.text:
Source: Standard textbooks and Wikipedia entries on measure theory, complex analysis, functional analysis, differential geometry, and algebraic topology.

Prerequisites: The corresponding branch for each branch. Every advanced route must list its prerequisites separately; it is not acceptable to gloss over them with "having studied mathematical analysis".

Advanced field Main content that must be completed before entry Connected chapters Measure theory and Lebesgue integration Countable operations on sets, real analysis, sequences of functions and convergence Sets, Spaces, Branches Axiomatic probability theory Measure theory and integration Advanced: Measure Theory Complex analysis Complex numbers, the relevant foundations of single-variable and multivariable analysis Number Systems, Spaces, Branches Functional analysis Linear algebra, metric spaces, normed spaces; some routes require measure and integration Algebra, Spaces, Advanced Differential geometry Multivariable calculus, linear algebra, foundations of topology Algebra, Spaces, Branches Algebraic topology Topology, group theory, and the corresponding algebraic tools Algebra, Branches Algebraic number theory Rings, fields, field extensions, and further algebra Algebra, Branches Analytic number theory Number theory, and the relevant parts of real and complex analysis Branches, Advanced Differential equations Linear algebra, calculus; deeper analysis added according to the topic Algebra, Spaces, Branches Optimization Linear algebra, calculus, foundations of convex analysis Algebra, Spaces, Branches Numerical analysis Linear algebra, calculus, error and stability Algebra, Spaces, Branches

docs.title: Entry Rules
docs.text:
1. Before measure theory: one must be able to handle countable unions/intersections, suprema, sequences of functions, and uniform convergence fluently; otherwise return first to the two chapters on sets and spaces.
  2. Before complex analysis: one must understand complex arithmetic, series, continuity, and differentiability; it is not sufficient to have studied limits only in the real case and then enter directly.
  3. Before functional analysis: one must master normed spaces, completeness, and linear operators; having studied only matrix computations is not enough.
  4. Before differential geometry: one must master multivariable differentiation, the implicit function theorem, linear algebra, and the foundations of topology.
  5. Before algebraic topology: one must master group theory (quotient groups, homomorphisms) and general topology (quotient spaces, compactness).
  6. Before axiomatic probability theory: measure theory must first be completed; one must not take "probability = frequency" as an axiom.

docs.title: Relations Among the Advanced Routes
docs.text:
• Measure theory is the foundation of axiomatic probability theory, functional analysis (in part), and harmonic analysis;
  • Complex analysis serves both analytic number theory and differential geometry/physics;
  • Algebraic topology depends on topology and group theory, and further connects to homological algebra;
  • Differential geometry depends on analysis, linear algebra, and topology, and further connects to geometric analysis;
  • Algebraic number theory depends on commutative algebra and field theory, while analytic number theory depends on complex analysis.

docs.title: Marking of Deferred Proofs
docs.text:
Some conclusions in advanced theory (such as the Riemann mapping theorem, Hahn–Banach, and Sylow's theorem) have very long proofs. The site permits:

  • Complete proof: all details are given;
  • Proof outline: the key steps and the dependencies are stated clearly;
  • Deferred proof: the page states explicitly "this page does not prove it for now; only the conclusion is used", and lists the required prerequisites.

What is not permitted is to use a conclusion directly as a definition without citing a source and without stating the prerequisites.

docs.title: 7.1 Measure and Integration: Core Results
docs.text:
A measure \(\mu\) on a measurable space \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\) satisfies:

  1. \(\mu(\varnothing)=0\);
  2. non-negativity;
  3. Countable additivity: if the \(A_i\) are pairwise disjoint, then \(\mu\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^\infty\mu(A_i)\).

Core convergence theorems (deferred proofs on this site; they require measure theory):

  • Monotone Convergence Theorem (MCT): if \(0\le f_n\uparrow f\) and the \(f_n\) are measurable, then \(\int f_n\to\int f\);
  • Fatou's Lemma: \(\int\liminf f_n\le\liminf\int f_n\);
  • Dominated Convergence Theorem (DCT): if the \(f_n\) are measurable, \(f_n\to f\) a.e., and \(|f_n|\le g\) with \(\int g<\infty\), then \(\int f_n\to\int f\).

These theorems are the formal conditions for "interchanging the integral and the limit"; the Riemann integral has no general theorem of comparable strength.

docs.title: 7.2 Complex Analysis: Core Results
docs.text:
• Cauchy's Integral Theorem: the integral of a holomorphic function around a closed path in a simply connected domain is 0;
  • Cauchy's Integral Formula: \(f(z)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}d\zeta\);
  • Liouville's Theorem: a bounded entire function is constant (this yields a proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra);
  • Residue Theorem: \(\oint_\gamma f(z)dz=2\pi i\sum\operatorname{Res}(f,z_k)\).

The heart of complex analysis is that "holomorphic" is far stronger than "real differentiable": holomorphic functions are automatically analytic and possess derivatives of all orders. The theorems above are deferred proofs on this site.

docs.title: 7.3 Functional Analysis: Core Results
docs.text:
• Hahn–Banach Theorem: under suitable conditions (a real or complex vector space, control by a sublinear functional or a seminorm), a linear functional can be extended with its norm preserved;
  • Open Mapping Theorem: a continuous linear surjection between Banach spaces is an open mapping;
  • Closed Graph Theorem: a linear mapping between Banach spaces whose graph is closed is bounded (continuous);
  • Uniform Boundedness Principle (Banach–Steinhaus): a family of linear operators that is pointwise bounded is uniformly bounded.

These theorems depend on completeness (Banach spaces) and cannot be used at the level of linear spaces alone; they are deferred proofs on this site.

docs.title: 7.4 Geometry and Topology: Core Results
docs.text:
• Gauss–Bonnet Theorem: the Euler characteristic of a compact surface is determined by the integral of the Gaussian curvature;
  • Fundamental Group: \(\pi_1(X,x_0)\) records the "holes" of a space;
  • Brouwer Fixed-Point Theorem: a continuous mapping from the closed unit ball in \(\mathbb R^n\) to itself has a fixed point;
  • Mayer–Vietoris: computes homology by means of a cover by subspaces.

docs.text:

  • Be able to list the three core prerequisites of complex analysis, functional analysis, and differential geometry, respectively.
  • Be able to explain the difference between a "deferred proof" and a "circular argument".

docs.title: Proof Status and Core Proofs
docs.text:
This page answers two questions: which theorems have complete proofs? Which are only stated/outlined?

Principle: an "idea of the proof" must not be written as a "proof". A complete proof must be checkable step by step; a deferred proof must be explicitly labeled and must list its prerequisites.

docs.title: Status Conventions
docs.text: Status Meaning Complete proof Starting from definitions/axioms, every step is given and checkable Proof outline The key constructions and steps are given, technical details are omitted; completeness is not claimed Deferred proof The page uses the conclusion only, leaving the proof to a later branch/textbook; prerequisites must be listed Definition/axiom Not used as a theorem proof, but as a starting point

docs.title: 1.1 De Morgan
docs.text:
We prove \( eg(P\land Q)\equiv eg P\lor eg Q\). Write out the truth table:

\(P\) \(Q\) \(P\land Q\) \( eg(P\land Q)\) \( eg P\lor eg Q\) T T T F F T F F T T F T F T T F F F T T

The two columns coincide, hence the equivalence. The equivalence \( eg(P\lor Q)\equiv eg P\land eg Q\) follows in the same way.

docs.title: 1.3 Quantifier Negation
docs.text:
By definition, \( orall x\in S,\ P(x)\) is false if and only if there exists \(x\in S\) for which \(P(x)\) is false:

\[ eg orall x\in S,\ P(x)\equiv\exists x\in S,\ eg P(x). \]

Likewise \( eg\exists x\in S,\ P(x)\equiv orall x\in S,\ eg P(x)\).

docs.title: 2. Equivalence Relation ↔ Partition
docs.text:
Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on \(A\). For each \(x\in A\), set \([x]=\{y\in A:x\sim y\}\).

Each step:

  1. Non-empty: by reflexivity, \(x\in[x]\).
  2. Pairwise disjoint or equal: if \([x]\cap[y]\ne\varnothing\), take \(z\in[x]\cap[y]\). Then \(x\sim z\) and \(y\sim z\). By symmetry \(z\sim y\), and by transitivity \(x\sim y\). For any \(w\in[x]\), \(w\sim x\sim y\), hence \(w\in[y]\); thus \([x]\subseteq[y]\). Similarly \([y]\subseteq[x]\), so \([x]=[y]\).
  3. Union is \(A\): every \(x\) belongs to \([x]\), so \(\bigcup_{x\in A}[x]=A\).

Therefore the equivalence classes form a partition.

Conversely, if \(\mathcal P\) is a partition of \(A\), define \(x\sim y\) if and only if \(x,y\) lie in the same block.

  • Reflexive: \(x\) lies in the same block as itself;
  • Symmetric: the relation of lying in the same block is symmetric;
  • Transitive: if \(x,y\) lie in the same block and \(y,z\) lie in the same block, then \(x,z\) lie in the same block.

Hence \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation, and its equivalence classes are exactly the blocks of the partition. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 3. Cantor's Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem: there is no surjection \(f:A o\mathcal P(A)\).

Proof: suppose for contradiction that \(f\) is a surjection. Define

\[ D=\{x\in A:x otin f(x)\}. \]

Then \(D\subseteq A\), that is, \(D\in\mathcal P(A)\). Since \(f\) is surjective, there exists \(d\in A\) with \(f(d)=D\).

Consider whether \(d\in D\):

  • If \(d\in D\), then by the definition of \(D\) we have \(d otin f(d)=D\), a contradiction;
  • If \(d otin D\), then \(d otin f(d)\), so by definition \(d\in D\), a contradiction.

Both cases lead to a contradiction, so no such surjection exists. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 4. Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein
docs.text:
Theorem: if there exist an injection \(f:A o B\) and an injection \(g:B o A\), then there exists a bijection \(h:A o B\).

Construction:

\[ C_0=A\setminus g(B),\qquad C_{n+1}=g(f(C_n)),\qquad C= igcup_{n=0}^\infty C_n. \]

Define

\[ h(x)= egin{cases} f(x), & x\in C,\ g^{-1}(x), & x otin C. \end{cases} \]

If \(x otin C\), then \(x otin C_0=A\setminus g(B)\), so \(x\in g(B)\), and \(g^{-1}(x)\) exists and is unique.

Well-defined: the two cases are mutually exclusive; \(g^{-1}(x)\) is unique.

Injective: suppose \(h(x)=h(y)\).

  • If \(x,y\in C\), then \(f(x)=f(y)\), and injectivity of \(f\) gives \(x=y\).
  • If \(x,y otin C\), then \(g^{-1}(x)=g^{-1}(y)\), which gives \(x=y\).
  • If \(x\in C,\ y otin C\), then \(f(x)=g^{-1}(y)\); applying \(g\) to both sides gives \(g(f(x))=y\). But \(x\in C_n\) for some \(n\), so \(g(f(x))\in C_{n+1}\subseteq C\), contradicting \(y otin C\).

Hence \(h\) is injective.

Surjective: take any \(y\in B\).

  • If \(g(y)\in C\), then \(g(y)\in C_{n+1}=g(f(C_n))\) for some \(n\) (note that \(g(y) otin C_0\)), so \(g(y)=g(f(c))\) for some \(c\in C_n\). By injectivity of \(g\), \(y=f(c)=h(c)\).
  • If \(g(y) otin C\), then \(h(g(y))=g^{-1}(g(y))=y\).

Hence \(h\) is surjective. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 5. Axiom of Choice, Zorn's Lemma, and the Well-Ordering Theorem
docs.text:
These three are equivalent (in ZF). This site does not prove this chain of equivalences; it requires ordinals, transfinite recursion, and an axiomatic system of set theory.

  • AC: every family of non-empty sets has a choice function;
  • Zorn: in a non-empty partially ordered set, if every chain has an upper bound, then there is a maximal element;
  • Well-ordering theorem: every set can be well ordered.

When using Zorn, one must verify that "every chain has an upper bound"; verifying only finite chains does not suffice.

docs.title: 6. Supremum Property of Dedekind Cuts
docs.text:
Let \(S\) be a family of non-empty Dedekind cuts bounded above by a cut \(B\) (that is, every \(A\in S\) satisfies \(A\subseteq B\)). Let

\[ U= igcup_{A\in S} A. \]

Proof that \(U\) is a cut:

  1. \(U e\varnothing\): \(S\) is non-empty; take \(A\in S\), then \(A e\varnothing\), so \(U\) is non-empty.
  2. \(U e\mathbb Q\): every \(A\subseteq B\), so \(U\subseteq B e\mathbb Q\).
  3. Downward closed: if \(q\in U\), then \(q\in A\) for some \(A\in S\); if \(p<q\), downward closure of \(A\) gives \(p\in A\subseteq U\).
  4. No greatest element: if \(q\in U\), then \(q\in A\) for some \(A\); \(A\) has no greatest element, so there exists \(r\in A\) with \(q<r\), whence \(r\in U\).

Therefore \(U\) is a cut.

Upper bound: every \(A\in S\) satisfies \(A\subseteq U\), so \(U\) is an upper bound.

Least upper bound: if \(C\) is any upper bound, then every \(A\subseteq C\), so \(U= igcup A\subseteq C\). Hence \(U\) is the least upper bound. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 7. Remaining Equivalent Forms of Completeness of the Reals
docs.text:
The number systems page lists five equivalent forms. This site gives a complete proof only of "Dedekind cuts ⇒ supremum property" (§6).

The remaining implications require the monotone bounded theorem, the nested interval theorem, and the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem from real analysis; they are proved in the spaces and branch-analysis sections. Here we do not repeatedly cite "equivalence" as a proved conclusion, but use it only as a roadmap.

docs.title: 8. Fundamental Theorem of Group Homomorphisms
docs.text:
Let \(\varphi:G\to H\) be a group homomorphism and \(K=\ker\varphi\).

The kernel is normal: for \(k\in K\) and \(g\in G\),

\[ \varphi(gkg^{-1})=\varphi(g)\varphi(k)\varphi(g)^{-1}=e, \]

so \(gkg^{-1}\in K\).

Definition: let \(\Phi:G/K\to\operatorname{im}\varphi\), \(\Phi(gK)=\varphi(g)\).

Well-defined: if \(gK=hK\), then \(h^{-1}g\in K\), so

\[ \varphi(h)^{-1}\varphi(g)=\varphi(h^{-1}g)=e, \]

hence \(\varphi(g)=\varphi(h)\).

Homomorphism:

\[ \Phi(gK\cdot hK)=\Phi(ghK)=\varphi(gh)=\varphi(g)\varphi(h)=\Phi(gK)\Phi(hK). \]

Injective: if \(\Phi(gK)=e\), then \(\varphi(g)=e\), so \(g\in K\), that is, \(gK=K\).

Surjective: take any \(y\in\operatorname{im}\varphi\); there exists \(g\) with \(y=\varphi(g)=\Phi(gK)\).

Therefore \(\Phi\) is an isomorphism, and \(G/K\cong\operatorname{im}\varphi\). This completes the proof.

docs.title: 9. Rank–Nullity Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(V\) be finite-dimensional and \(T:V\to W\) linear. Take a basis of \(\ker T\),

\[ v_1,\dots,v_k. \]

Extend it to a basis of \(V\),

\[ v_1,\dots,v_k,v_{k+1},\dots,v_n. \]

Proof that \(T(v_{k+1}),\dots,T(v_n)\) is a basis of \(\operatorname{im}T\):

Spanning: take any \(v=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i\); then

\[ T(v)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_iT(v_i)=\sum_{i=k+1}^n a_iT(v_i), \]

because the first \(k\) terms lie in the kernel.

Linear independence: if \(\sum_{i=k+1}^n a_iT(v_i)=0\), then

\[ T\left(\sum_{i=k+1}^n a_iv_i\right)=0, \]

so \(\sum_{i=k+1}^n a_iv_i\in\ker T\). But this is also a combination of \(v_{k+1},\dots,v_n\); the kernel has basis \(v_1,\dots,v_k\). By linear independence of a basis, all \(a_i=0\).

Therefore \(\dim\operatorname{im}T=n-k\), that is,

\[ \dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T. \]

This completes the proof.

docs.title: 10. Open Balls Are Open Sets
docs.text:
Let \(y\in B(x,r)\) and set \(s=r-d(x,y)>0\). For any \(z\in B(y,s)\), the triangle inequality gives

\[ d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)<d(x,y)+s=r, \]

so \(z\in B(x,r)\). Hence \(B(y,s)\subseteq B(x,r)\), that is, \(B(x,r)\) is an open set. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 11. Two Characterizations of Continuity
docs.text: Let \(f:X\to Y\), where \(X,Y\) are metric spaces.

docs.title: ε-δ ⇒ Preimage of an Open Set Is Open
docs.text:
Let \(V\subseteq Y\) be open and \(x\in f^{-1}(V)\). Then \(f(x)\in V\), so there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(B_Y(f(x),\varepsilon)\subseteq V\). By continuity, there exists \(\delta>0\) such that

\[ f(B_X(x,\delta))\subseteq B_Y(f(x),\varepsilon)\subseteq V. \]

Hence \(B_X(x,\delta)\subseteq f^{-1}(V)\), that is, \(f^{-1}(V)\) is open.

docs.title: Preimage of an Open Set Is Open ⇒ ε-δ
docs.text: Given \(x\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), take \(V=B_Y(f(x),\varepsilon)\). \(V\) is open, so \(f^{-1}(V)\) is open and contains \(x\). There exists \(\delta>0\) with \(B_X(x,\delta)\subseteq f^{-1}(V)\), that is, \(f(B_X(x,\delta))\subseteq V\). This is precisely the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 12. Continuous Image of a Compact Set Is Compact
docs.text:
Let \(f:X\to Y\) be continuous and \(X\) compact. Take any open cover \(\{V_i\}_{i\in I}\) of \(f(X)\). Then

\[ \{f^{-1}(V_i)\}_{i\in I} \]

is an open cover of \(X\). Since \(X\) is compact, there is a finite subcover

\[ X=f^{-1}(V_{i_1})\cup\cdots\cup f^{-1}(V_{i_m}). \]

Thus

\[ f(X)\subseteq V_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{i_m}. \]

Therefore \(f(X)\) is compact. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 13. Extreme Value Theorem on Compact Sets
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be non-empty and compact, and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. By §12, \(f(X)\) is a compact subset of \(\mathbb R\), hence bounded and closed.

Let \(M=\sup f(X)\). By the definition of supremum, there exist \(x_n\in X\) with \(f(x_n)\to M\). Since \(f(X)\) is closed, \(M\in f(X)\), so there exists \(x\in X\) with \(f(x)=M\). The argument for the minimum is the same. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 15. Banach Contraction Mapping Principle
docs.text:
Theorem: let \((X,d)\) be complete and let \(T:X\to X\) satisfy

\[ d(Tx,Ty)\le q\,d(x,y),\qquad 0\le q<1. \]

Then \(T\) has a unique fixed point.

Existence: take any \(x_0\in X\) and set \(x_{n+1}=T(x_n)\). Induction gives

\[ d(x_{n+1},x_{n+2})\le q\,d(x_n,x_{n+1})\le q^{n+1}d(x_0,x_1). \]

For \(m>n\), the triangle inequality and the geometric series give

\[ d(x_n,x_m)\le\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}d(x_k,x_{k+1}) \le d(x_0,x_1)\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}q^k \le \frac{q^n}{1-q}d(x_0,x_1)\to0. \]

So \(\{x_n\}\) is a Cauchy sequence. Since \(X\) is complete, \(x_n\to x\). By continuity of \(T\) (Lipschitz implies continuous),

\[ T(x)=\lim T(x_n)=\lim x_{n+1}=x. \]

Uniqueness: if \(x,y\) are both fixed points, then

\[ d(x,y)=d(Tx,Ty)\le q\,d(x,y), \]

and since \(0\le q<1\), necessarily \(d(x,y)=0\), that is, \(x=y\). This completes the proof.

docs.title: Chapter 1 · The Real and Complex Number Systems
docs.text:
Source: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Chapter 1; the number-systems chapter of the Regular System.

Rudin route: this chapter is Chapter 1 of the analysis route; Chapters 2–11 have already been developed. Prerequisites: propositional logic, sets and mappings, and the basic language of ordered fields. Goal of this chapter: to raise "the real numbers are complete, the complex numbers admit arithmetic, and Euclidean space carries an inner product" from intuition to provable theorems.

← Theory Overview Spaces, Limits, and Continuity Proof Status

docs.title: 1.1 Ordered Fields
docs.text:
Field \((F,+,\cdot)\): \((F,+)\) is an abelian group, \((F\setminus\{0\},\cdot)\) is an abelian group, and multiplication distributes over addition.

Ordered field: there exists a total order \(\le\) such that

\[ x\le y\Rightarrow x+z\le y+z, \] \[ 0\le x,\ 0\le y\Rightarrow 0\le xy. \]

We write \(x<y\) to mean \(x\le y\) and \(x\ne y\).

docs.title: Theorem 1.1 (Basic Consequences of an Ordered Field)
docs.text:
Let \(x,y,z\in F\).

  1. If \(x+y=x+z\), then \(y=z\);
  2. If \(x+y=0\), then \(y=-x\);
  3. \((-x)y=-(xy)\), \((-x)(-y)=xy\);
  4. If \(x e0\), then \(x^{-1} e0\), and \((x^{-1})^{-1}=x\);
  5. \(0<x\iff -x<0\);
  6. If \(x>0,y>0\), then \(xy>0\); if \(x>0\), then \(x^{-1}>0\).

Proof:

Step 1: add \(-x\) to both sides,

\[ egin{aligned} y &= 0+y=(-x+x)+y\ &= -x+(x+y)=-x+(x+z)\ &= (-x+x)+z=z. \end{aligned} \]

Step 2: by Step 1, \(x+y=x+(-x)=0\), hence \(y=-x\).

Step 3: by the distributive law,

\[ 0=x\cdot0=x(y+(-y))=xy+x(-y), \]

so \(x(-y)=-(xy)\). Then \((-x)y=-(xy)\) yields \((-x)(-y)=xy\).

Step 4: if \(x^{-1}=0\), then \(1=xx^{-1}=0\), a contradiction; hence \(x^{-1} e0\). Also \(x^{-1}x=1\), so \((x^{-1})^{-1}=x\).

Step 5: \(0<x\iff -x<0\): it suffices to add \(-x\) to both sides.

Step 6: by the ordering, \(0<x,0<y\Rightarrow0<xy\). If \(x^{-1}<0\), then \(xx^{-1}<0\) (multiplying a positive \(x\) by a negative number), that is, \(1<0\), which contradicts \(1>0\); hence \(x^{-1}>0\).

This completes the proof.

docs.title: 1.2 Suprema and Completeness
docs.text:
Let \(S\subseteq F\) be nonempty.

  • \(u\) is an upper bound of \(S\): \(\forall s\in S,\ s\le u\);
  • \(u\) is the supremum \(\sup S\): \(u\) is an upper bound, and every upper bound \(v\) satisfies \(u\le v\);
  • lower bounds and the infimum \(\inf S\) are defined dually.

Lemma 1.2 (Uniqueness of the Supremum): if \(\sup S\) exists, then it is unique.

Proof: if \(u,u'\) are both suprema, then \(u\) is an upper bound and \(u'\) is the least upper bound, so \(u'\le u\); likewise \(u\le u'\). By antisymmetry, \(u=u'\). This completes the proof.

Least-upper-bound property (LUB): every nonempty subset that is bounded above has a supremum. Starting from an ordered field, Rudin takes LUB as the completeness axiom for, or construction result of, the real number system; the number systems on this site prove it by Dedekind cuts.

Archimedean property: for any \(x,y>0\) there exists \(n\in\mathbb N\) such that \(nx>y\).

docs.title: 1.3 The Archimedean Property and Density of the Rationals
Theorem 1.3 (Archimedean)
docs.text:
If \(x,y\in\mathbb R\) and \(x>0\), then there exists a positive integer \(n\) such that \(nx>y\).

Proof: suppose, to the contrary, that \(nx\le y\) for all \(n\in\mathbb N\). Then \(\mathbb N\) has the upper bound \(y/x\). By LUB, \(\alpha=\sup\mathbb N\) exists.

Since \(\alpha-1\) is not an upper bound, there exists \(n\in\mathbb N\) such that \(n>\alpha-1\). Then \(n+1>\alpha\), but \(n+1\in\mathbb N\), contradicting the fact that \(\alpha\) is an upper bound. This completes the proof.

Corollary 1.4: \(\mathbb N\) is unbounded in \(\mathbb R\); for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(n\) such that \(1/n<\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Theorem 1.5 (Density of the Rationals)
docs.text:
If \(x<y\) are real numbers, then there exists \(q\in\mathbb Q\) such that \(x<q<y\).

Proof: by the Archimedean property, choose a positive integer \(n\) such that

\[ n(y-x)>1. \]

Let \(m\) be the least integer satisfying \(m>nx\) (well-ordering of the integers). Then

\[ m-1\le nx<m. \]

From \(m>nx\) we get \(x<m/n\). Also \(m\le nx+1<ny\), so \(m/n<y\). Hence \(m/n\in(x,y)\cap\mathbb Q\). This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 1.6 (n-th Roots of Positive Real Numbers)
docs.text:
If \(x>0\), \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(n\ge1\), then there exists a unique \(y>0\) such that \(y^n=x\). We write \(y=x^{1/n}\).

Existence: let

\[ S=\{t\ge0:t^n<x\}. \]

Then \(0\in S\), and \(1+x\) is an upper bound (if \(t>1+x\), then \(t^n>(1+x)^n\ge1+x>x\)). Let \(y=\sup S\).

We prove that \(y^n=x\), distinguishing two cases.

Case 1: \(y^n<x\). Choose \(0<h<1\) small enough that

\[ n(y+1)^{n-1}h<x-y^n. \]

By the binomial expansion,

\[ (y+h)^n\le y^n+n(y+1)^{n-1}h<x, \]

so \(y+h\in S\), contradicting the fact that \(y\) is an upper bound.

Case 2: \(y^n>x\). Choose \(0<h<y\) small enough that

\[ ny^{n-1}h<y^n-x. \]

By Bernoulli's inequality,

\[ (y-h)^n\ge y^n-ny^{n-1}h>x, \]

so \(y-h\) is also an upper bound, contradicting the fact that \(y\) is the least upper bound.

Therefore necessarily \(y^n=x\).

Uniqueness: if \(y_1^n=y_2^n=x\) with \(y_1,y_2>0\), then \(y_1=y_2\) (the function \(t\mapsto t^n\) is strictly increasing for \(t>0\)). This completes the proof.

docs.title: 1.5 Absolute Value and the Triangle Inequality
docs.text:
Define

\[ |x|= \begin{cases} x,&x\ge0,\\ -x,&x<0. \end{cases} \]

Properties:

\[ |xy|=|x||y|,\qquad |x|^2=x^2,\qquad |x|\le a\iff -a\le x\le a\ (a\ge0). \]

docs.title: Theorem 1.7 (Triangle Inequality)
docs.text:
\[ |x+y|\le|x|+|y|. \]

Proof: from \(-|x|\le x\le|x|\) and \(-|y|\le y\le|y|\), adding gives

\[ -(|x|+|y|)\le x+y\le|x|+|y|, \]

that is, \(|x+y|\le|x|+|y|\). This completes the proof.

Corollary: \(||x|-|y||\le|x-y|\).

docs.title: 1.6 The Complex Field
docs.text:
Define the complex numbers as ordered pairs \((a,b)\in\mathbb R^2\), with the operations

\[ (a,b)+(c,d)=(a+c,b+d), \] \[ (a,b)(c,d)=(ac-bd,\ ad+bc). \]

Writing \(i=(0,1)\), we have \(i^2=(-1,0)=-1\), and \((a,b)=a+bi\).

docs.title: Theorem 1.8 (The Complex Field)
docs.text:
\(\mathbb C\) is a field under the above operations; \(\mathbb R\) embeds in \(\mathbb C\) via \(a\mapsto(a,0)\).

Proof:

Addition: adding componentwise gives an abelian group, with zero element \((0,0)\) and inverse \((-a,-b)\).

Multiplication: commutativity, associativity and distributivity follow directly from the corresponding properties of real arithmetic; the identity element is \((1,0)\).

Inverses: for a nonzero element \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\), let

\[ (a,b)^{-1}=\left(\frac{a}{a^2+b^2},\frac{-b}{a^2+b^2}\right). \]

We verify that the product is \((1,0)\):

\[ (a,b)\left(\frac{a}{a^2+b^2},\frac{-b}{a^2+b^2}\right) =\left(\frac{a^2+b^2}{a^2+b^2},\frac{-ab+ba}{a^2+b^2}\right)=(1,0). \]

Hence \(\mathbb C\) is a field; the embedding \(a\mapsto(a,0)\) preserves addition and multiplication, so \(\mathbb R\subseteq\mathbb C\). This completes the proof.

Conjugation and modulus:

\[ \overline{a+bi}=a-bi,\qquad |z|^2=z\overline z=a^2+b^2. \] \[ \overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad |zw|=|z||w|. \]

docs.title: 1.7 Euclidean Spaces and the Schwarz Inequality
docs.text:
For \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n),y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)\in\mathbb R^n\), define

\[ x\cdot y=\sum_{i=1}^n x_iy_i,\qquad \|x\|=\sqrt{x\cdot x}. \]

docs.title: Theorem 1.9 (Cauchy–Schwarz)
docs.text:
\[ |x\cdot y|\le\|x\|\|y\|. \]

Proof: if \(y=0\), both sides are 0. Otherwise, for any \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\),

\[ 0\le\|x-\lambda y\|^2 =\|x\|^2-2\lambda(x\cdot y)+\lambda^2\|y\|^2. \]

Taking \(\lambda=\dfrac{x\cdot y}{\|y\|^2}\) gives

\[ 0\le\|x\|^2-\frac{(x\cdot y)^2}{\|y\|^2}, \]

that is, \((x\cdot y)^2\le\|x\|^2\|y\|^2\). Taking square roots yields \(|x\cdot y|\le\|x\|\|y\|\). This completes the proof.

Corollary (triangle inequality):

\[ \|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|. \]

Proof: expand \(\|x+y\|^2\) and estimate the cross term by Schwarz.

docs.title: 1.8 Proof Status for This Chapter
docs.text:
Result Status Basic consequences of ordered fields Complete proof Uniqueness of the supremum Complete proof Archimedean property Complete proof (using LUB) Density of the rationals Complete proof (using Archimedean property + well-ordering of the integers) n-th roots of positive real numbers Complete proof (using LUB + binomial/Bernoulli estimates) Triangle inequality Complete proof The complex field Complete proof (verification of operations + inverse formula) Cauchy–Schwarz Complete proof

LUB itself is proved by Dedekind cuts in the number systems; this chapter uses it as a completeness property of the real number system.

docs.text:

docs.text:
• Regular System: logic, sets, number systems, algebra;
  • Spaces, Limits, and Continuity: metric spaces, convergence, and the basic language of continuity.

docs.title: 2.1 Metric Spaces
docs.text:
A metric space is a set \(X\) equipped with a function \(d:X\times X\to[0,\infty)\) satisfying

\[ d(x,y)=0\iff x=y,\qquad d(x,y)=d(y,x),\qquad d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z). \]

Open ball:

\[ B(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}. \]

Open set: \(U\subseteq X\) is open if for every \(x\in U\) there exists \(r>0\) such that \(B(x,r)\subseteq U\). Closed set: the complement is open.

docs.title: Theorem 2.1 (Every Open Ball Is Open)
docs.text:
Every open ball \(B(x,r)\) is an open set.

Proof: Let \(y\in B(x,r)\) and set \(s=r-d(x,y)>0\). For any \(z\in B(y,s)\),

\[ d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)<d(x,y)+s=r, \]

hence \(B(y,s)\subseteq B(x,r)\). This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 2.2 (Closed Sets ↔ Open Sets)
docs.text:
\(F\subseteq X\) is closed \(\iff F^c\) is open.

Proof: By definition, \(F\) is closed precisely when \(F^c\) is open; the converse holds likewise. This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 2.3 (Characterisation of the Closure)
docs.text:
Let \(E\subseteq X\). Then

\[ \overline E=E\cup E', \]

where \(E'\) is the set of limit points of \(E\). Moreover, \(x\in\overline E\) if and only if every \(B(x,r)\) meets \(E\).

Proof outline: If \(x\in\overline E\) and some \(B(x,r)\cap E=\varnothing\), then \(E\subseteq B(x,r)^c\), and \(B(x,r)^c\) is closed, so \(\overline E\subseteq B(x,r)^c\), a contradiction. Conversely, if every ball meets \(E\), then \(x\) belongs to every closed set containing \(E\), hence \(x\in\overline E\). The details are supplied from the definition of a closed set.

docs.title: 2.2 Compactness
docs.text: Open cover: \(\{U_i\}\) is an open cover of \(K\) if \(K\subseteq\bigcup_i U_i\). Compact: every open cover has a finite subcover.

docs.title: Theorem 2.4 (Compact Sets Are Closed)
docs.text:
A compact set \(K\) in a metric space is closed.

Proof: Take \(p\notin K\). For each \(q\in K\), set \(r_q=d(p,q)/2>0\). The balls \(B(q,r_q)\) cover \(K\); by compactness there exist finitely many \(q_1,\dots,q_m\) such that

\[ K\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^m B(q_j,r_{q_j}). \]

Let

\[ \rho=\min_{1\le j\le m} d(p,q_j)>0. \]

Then \(B(p,\rho/2)\) is disjoint from every \(B(q_j,r_{q_j})\), hence disjoint from \(K\). Therefore \(p\) is not in the closure, and \(K\) is closed. This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 2.5 (Compact Sets Are Bounded)
docs.text:
A compact set \(K\) is bounded: there exist \(p\in X\) and \(R>0\) such that \(K\subseteq B(p,R)\).

Proof: Choose any \(p\in X\). The family of balls \(\{B(p,n):n\in\mathbb N\}\) covers \(K\); compactness yields a finite subcover, and we take \(R\) to be the largest radius. This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 2.6 (Closed Subsets of Compact Sets Are Compact)
docs.text:
If \(K\) is compact and \(F\subseteq K\) is closed (in \(X\)), then \(F\) is compact.

Proof: Take an open cover \(\{U_i\}\) of \(F\). Adjoining \(F^c\) yields an open cover of \(K\); since \(K\) is compact, we extract a finite subcover. Removing \(F^c\), the remaining sets \(U_i\) cover \(F\). This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 2.7 (Heine–Borel, R^n)
docs.text:
\(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is compact \(\iff K\) is bounded and closed.

Proof status: the full proof is deferred; it requires the completeness of \(\mathbb R^n\), the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem, and a finite-subcover argument. The idea of the proof is "bounded closed set \(\Rightarrow\) sequentially compact \(\Rightarrow\) compact", where sequential compactness is obtained by coordinate bisection.

docs.title: 2.3 Connectedness
docs.text: Separation: \(X=A\cup B\), with \(A,B\) non-empty, disjoint, and both open (equivalently, both closed). Connected: no such separation exists.

docs.title: Theorem 2.8 (Connected Subsets of R Are Intervals)
docs.text:
\(E\subseteq\mathbb R\) is connected \(\iff E\) is an interval.

Proof: If \(E\) is not an interval, there exist \(a<b<c\) with \(a,c\in E\) and \(b\notin E\). Then

\[ E=(E\cap(-\infty,b))\cup(E\cap(b,\infty)) \]

is a union of non-empty disjoint open sets (in the relative topology), hence disconnected.

Conversely, suppose \(E\) is an interval and \(E=A\cup B\) is a separation. Take \(a\in A,b\in B\), and assume without loss of generality that \(a<b\). Let

\[ c=\sup(A\cap[a,b]). \]

Since \(A\) is relatively closed, \(c\in A\); since \(B\) is relatively open, for \(c<b\) we have \(c+\varepsilon\in B\) for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), which makes \(A\cap[a,b]\) admit a larger upper bound, a contradiction; if \(c=b\), then \(b\in A\cap B\), again a contradiction. Therefore \(E\) is connected. This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 2.9 (Continuous Images of Connected Sets)
docs.text:
A continuous mapping sends connected sets to connected sets.

Proof: If \(f(E)=A\cup B\) is a separation, then \(E=f^{-1}(A)\cup f^{-1}(B)\) is a separation (the preimage of an open set under a continuous mapping is open), a contradiction. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 2.4 The Cantor Set
docs.text:
Begin with \([0,1]\) and delete the middle third at each step:

\[ C_0=[0,1],\quad C_1=[0,\tfrac13]\cup[\tfrac23,1],\quad C_{n+1}\subset C_n, \]

and let

\[ C=\bigcap_{n=0}^\infty C_n. \]

Properties:

  1. \(C\) is compact and non-empty;
  2. \(C\) is perfect (it has no isolated points);
  3. \(C\) is nowhere dense;
  4. \(C\) is uncountable.

Idea of the uncountability proof: the points whose ternary expansion uses only the digits \(0,1,2\) but never \(1\) belong to \(C\); encoding a \(0/2\) sequence as a binary sequence yields \(2^{\aleph_0}\) points. Distinct binary sequences give distinct points (apart from countably many points of ternary ambiguity), so \(C\) is uncountable.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
1. Prove that the union of finitely many compact sets is compact, and that the intersection of arbitrarily many closed sets is closed.
  2. In a discrete metric space, which sets are compact? Which sets are connected?
  3. Prove that \(\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]\) is not compact (construct an open cover with no finite subcover).

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
1. Prove that every infinite subset of a compact metric space has a limit point.
  2. Prove that the continuous image of a connected set is connected; give an example of a connected set whose image under a continuous mapping is not closed.
  3. Prove that the Cantor set has no isolated points and is nowhere dense.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
1. Prove that the Cantor set is uncountable, and explain its cardinality relation to \(2^{\mathbb N}\).
  2. Prove that in a metric space, "compact \(\iff\) sequentially compact \(\iff\) complete and totally bounded". (This may be completed after the BW theorem in Chapter 3.)

Hint: for Exercise 8, first prove "compact \(\Rightarrow\) sequentially compact" by contradiction using open covers; then prove "sequentially compact \(\Rightarrow\) complete and totally bounded"; finally, use total boundedness together with completeness to construct a finite subcover.

docs.title: Chapter 3 · Sequences and Series

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Logic, sets, number systems;
  • Chapter 2: metric spaces, compactness;
  • Spaces, Limits, and Continuity: the preliminary language of convergence of sequences.

docs.title: 3.1 Convergence and Basic Properties
docs.text:
A sequence \(\{a_n\}\subseteq\mathbb R\) converges to \(a\) if

\[ \forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists N,\ \forall n>N:\ |a_n-a|<\varepsilon. \]

docs.title: Theorem 3.1 (Uniqueness of the Limit)
docs.text:
A convergent sequence has a unique limit.

Proof: Suppose \(a_n\to a\) and \(a_n\to b\), and take \(\varepsilon=|a-b|/2\) (if \(a\ne b\)). There exists \(N\) such that for \(n>N\) we have \(|a_n-a|<\varepsilon\) and \(|a_n-b|<\varepsilon\). Then

\[ |a-b|\le|a-a_n|+|a_n-b|<2\varepsilon=|a-b|, \]

a contradiction. Hence \(a=b\). Q.E.D.

docs.title: Theorem 3.2 (Convergent ⇒ Bounded)
docs.text:
A convergent sequence is bounded.

Proof: Take \(\varepsilon=1\); there exists \(N\) such that \(|a_n-a|<1\) for \(n>N\). Put

\[ M=\max\{|a_1|,\dots,|a_N|,|a|+1\}, \]

then \(|a_n|\le M\) for every term. Q.E.D.

docs.title: Theorem 3.3 (Monotone and Bounded ⇒ Convergent)
docs.text:
If \(\{a_n\}\) is monotonically increasing and bounded above, then \(a_n\to\sup\{a_n\}\).

Proof: Let \(L=\sup\{a_n\}\). For any \(\varepsilon>0\), \(L-\varepsilon\) is not an upper bound, so there exists \(N\) with \(a_N>L-\varepsilon\). By monotonicity, for \(n>N\),

\[ L-\varepsilon<a_N\le a_n\le L, \]

hence \(|a_n-L|<\varepsilon\). Q.E.D.

docs.title: 3.2 Subsequences, Cauchy Sequences, and Completeness
docs.text: Subsequence: \(\{a_{n_k}\}\), where \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\).

docs.title: Theorem 3.4 (Convergent ⇒ Subsequences Converge)
docs.text:
If \(a_n\to a\), then every subsequence also converges to \(a\).

Proof: Given \(\varepsilon>0\), take the \(N\) of the original sequence; since \(n_k\ge k\), for \(k>N\) we have \(n_k>N\), hence \(|a_{n_k}-a|<\varepsilon\). Q.E.D.

Cauchy sequence:

\[ \forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists N,\ \forall m,n>N:\ |a_m-a_n|<\varepsilon. \]

docs.title: Theorem 3.5 (Cauchy Criterion)
docs.text:
A sequence in \(\mathbb R\) converges \(\iff\) it is a Cauchy sequence.

Proof outline:

  • Convergent ⇒ Cauchy: use the triangle inequality;
  • Cauchy ⇒ bounded: take \(\varepsilon=1\); only finitely many terms lie outside the interval;
  • By Bolzano–Weierstrass, extract a convergent subsequence \(a_{n_k}\to a\);
  • Use the Cauchy property together with the convergence of the subsequence to prove \(a_n\to a\).

The complete proof depends on BW; this site marks BW as deferred (see below).

docs.title: Theorem 3.6 (Bolzano–Weierstrass)
docs.text:
Every bounded sequence in \(\mathbb R^n\) has a convergent subsequence.

Proof status: Complete proof deferred. The usual method: repeatedly bisect the interval, choosing the half containing infinitely many terms, to obtain nested intervals; take the intersection point by the nested interval theorem, then extract a subsequence.

docs.title: 3.3 Limit Superior and Limit Inferior
docs.text:
\[ \limsup_{n\to\infty}a_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{k\ge n}a_k, \qquad \liminf_{n\to\infty}a_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{k\ge n}a_k. \]

The values \(\pm\infty\) are allowed. If \((a_n)\) is bounded, then \(\limsup a_n\) is the largest subsequential limit and \(\liminf a_n\) is the smallest subsequential limit.

docs.title: Theorem 3.7 (Convergence ↔ Equality of Limit Superior and Limit Inferior)
docs.text:
A bounded sequence \(\{a_n\}\) converges \(\iff\)

\[ \liminf a_n=\limsup a_n. \]

In that case the limit equals the common value.

Proof outline: If the sequence converges to \(a\), then both the suprema and the infima of the tails tend to \(a\); conversely, if the limit superior and the limit inferior both equal \(a\), the definition yields a squeeze.

docs.title: 3.4 Series
docs.text:
The series \(\sum a_n\) converges if the partial sums

\[ s_n=a_1+\cdots+a_n \]

converge.

docs.title: Theorem 3.8 (Necessary Condition for Convergence)
docs.text:
If \(\sum a_n\) converges, then \(a_n\to0\).

Proof: \(a_n=s_n-s_{n-1}\to s-s=0\). Q.E.D.

The converse fails: the harmonic series \(\sum 1/n\) diverges.

docs.title: Theorem 3.9 (Absolute Convergence ⇒ Convergence)
docs.text:
If \(\sum|a_n|\) converges, then \(\sum a_n\) converges.

Proof: Let \(p_n=\max(a_n,0)\) and \(q_n=\max(-a_n,0)\). Then \(0\le p_n,q_n\le|a_n|\), so by the comparison test \(\sum p_n,\sum q_n\) converge; since \(a_n=p_n-q_n\), it follows that \(\sum a_n\) converges. Q.E.D.

docs.title: Theorem 3.10 (Ratio and Root Tests)
docs.text:
Suppose \(a_n\ne0\).

  • If \(\limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n|<1\), then \(\sum a_n\) converges absolutely;
  • If \(\liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n|>1\), then \(\sum a_n\) diverges;
  • If \(\limsup |a_n|^{1/n}<1\), then the series converges absolutely;
  • If \(\limsup |a_n|^{1/n}>1\), then the series diverges.

Proof outline: Compare with a geometric series; for the root test, \(|a_n|^{1/n}\le q<1\) yields \(|a_n|\le q^n\).

docs.title: Theorem 3.11 (Power Series)
docs.text:
For a power series \(\sum c_n x^n\), there exists a radius of convergence \(R\in[0,\infty]\) such that

\[ |x|<R\Rightarrow\text{absolute convergence},\qquad |x|>R\Rightarrow\text{divergence}. \]

Moreover,

\[ \frac1R=\limsup_{n\to\infty}|c_n|^{1/n}. \]

The series converges uniformly on compact subsets of \(|x|<R\).

Proof outline: Apply the root test to \(\sum c_nx^n\); uniform convergence on compact subsets follows from the Weierstrass test (Chapter 7).

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
1. Find the limit: \(\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{3n^2+2}{n^2-n}\).
  2. Prove: if \(a_n\to a\), then \(|a_n|\to|a|\); is the converse true?
  3. Determine the convergence of the series \(\sum \frac{1}{n^2}\), \(\sum \frac{1}{n}\), \(\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}\).

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
1. Prove that \(\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{1/n}=1\).
  2. Find the radius of convergence and the interval of convergence of \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n}\).
  3. Give an example of a bounded sequence that does not converge, yet for which \(\limsup\) and \(\liminf\) both exist and are unequal.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
1. Prove: if \(\sum a_n\) converges absolutely, then every rearrangement converges to the same value.
  2. Prove: if \(a_n>0\) and \(\sum a_n\) converges, then \(\sum \sqrt{a_n}/n\) converges (hint: Cauchy–Schwarz).

Hint: In Exercise 8, pair \(\sqrt{a_n}\) with \(1/n\), estimate by finite sums, and then pass to the limit.

docs.title: Chapter 4 · Continuity
docs.text: Status: Expanded. Core theorems are either proved or explicitly marked "deferred". Part of: Rudin System · Chapter 4 · Continuity Source: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Chapter 4.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Sets and number systems;
  • Chapter 2: compactness, connectedness;
  • Spaces, Limits, and Continuity: the preliminary definitions of metric spaces and continuous mappings.

docs.title: 4.1 Limits of Functions
docs.text:
Let \(E\subseteq X\), let \(f:E\to Y\), and let \(p\) be a limit point of \(E\). We write

\[ \lim_{x\to p}f(x)=q \]

if

\[ \forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists\delta>0,\ 0<d_X(x,p)<\delta\Rightarrow d_Y(f(x),q)<\varepsilon. \]

Continuity: \(f\) is continuous at \(p\in E\) if \(\lim_{x\to p}f(x)=f(p)\) (when \(p\) is an isolated point it is automatically continuous).

docs.title: Theorem 4.1 (Continuity ↔ Sequential Continuity)
docs.text:
\(f\) is continuous at \(p\) \(\iff\) for every \(x_n\to p\) (with \(x_n\in E\)), we have \(f(x_n)\to f(p)\).

Proof sketch:

  • Continuity ⇒ sequences: use the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition;
  • Sequences ⇒ continuity: suppose not; then there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every \(n\) one can choose \(x_n\) with \(d(x_n,p)<1/n\) but \(d(f(x_n),f(p))\ge\varepsilon\), contradicting sequential continuity.

docs.title: Theorem 4.2 (Composition of Continuous Maps)
docs.text:
If \(f:X\to Y\) is continuous at \(p\) and \(g:Y\to Z\) is continuous at \(f(p)\), then \(g\circ f\) is continuous at \(p\).

Proof: Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(\eta>0\) such that \(d_Y(y,f(p))<\eta\Rightarrow d_Z(g(y),g(f(p)))<\varepsilon\); then choose \(\delta>0\) such that \(d_X(x,p)<\delta\Rightarrow d_Y(f(x),f(p))<\eta\). This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 4.3 (Continuous Image of a Compact Set)
docs.text:
A continuous mapping carries compact sets to compact sets, and connected sets to connected sets.

Proof: For the compact part see proof page §12; for the connected part see Theorem 2.9 of Chapter 2. This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 4.4 (Extreme Value Theorem)
docs.text:
A real-valued continuous function on a non-empty compact set is bounded and attains its maximum and minimum.

Proof: See proof page §13.

docs.title: Theorem 4.5 (Intermediate Value Theorem)
docs.text:
If \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and \(f(a)<c<f(b)\), then there exists \(\xi\in(a,b)\) such that \(f(\xi)=c\).

Proof: Let \(S=\{x\in[a,b]:f(x)<c\}\). \(S\) is non-empty and bounded above; let \(\xi=\sup S\). By continuity, \(f(\xi)\le c\). If \(f(\xi)<c\), then \(f(x)<c\) still holds in a neighbourhood of \(\xi\), contradicting that \(\xi\) is an upper bound. Hence \(f(\xi)=c\). This completes the proof.

docs.title: 4.3 Uniform Continuity
docs.text:
\(f:X\to Y\) is uniformly continuous if

\[ \forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists\delta>0,\ \forall x,y\in X:\ d_X(x,y)<\delta\Rightarrow d_Y(f(x),f(y))<\varepsilon. \]

docs.title: Theorem 4.6 (Continuous on a Compact Set ⇒ Uniformly Continuous)
docs.text:
A continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous.

Proof sketch: Given \(\varepsilon>0\), for each \(p\) choose \(\delta_p\) such that \(f(B(p,\delta_p))\subseteq B(f(p),\varepsilon/2)\). The balls \(B(p,\delta_p/2)\) cover \(X\); take a finite subcover \(p_1,\dots,p_m\) and set \(\delta=\min\delta_{p_i}/2\). If \(d(x,y)<\delta\), choose \(p_i\) with \(x\in B(p_i,\delta_{p_i}/2)\); then \(y\in B(p_i,\delta_{p_i})\), so that \(d(f(x),f(y))<\varepsilon\).

docs.title: 4.4 Points of Discontinuity and Monotone Functions
docs.text: Discontinuity of the first kind: both one-sided limits exist; of the second kind: at least one of them fails to exist. Jump discontinuity: both one-sided limits exist but are unequal.

docs.title: Theorem 4.7 (Points of Discontinuity of a Monotone Function)
docs.text:
A monotone function on an interval has at most countably many points of discontinuity, and all of them are jump discontinuities.

Proof sketch: Each point of discontinuity \(x\) corresponds to a non-empty open interval \((f(x-),f(x+))\); distinct points of discontinuity correspond to disjoint intervals, and each interval contains a rational number, so there are at most countably many.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
1. Use the definition to prove that \(f(x)=x^2\) is continuous on \(\mathbb R\).
  2. Determine whether \(f(x)=1/x\) is uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\).
  3. Find the limit of \(f(x)=\sin(1/x)\) at \(x=0\); state whether it admits a continuous extension.

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
1. Prove that a continuous function carries connected sets to connected sets.
  2. Prove that if \(f\) is continuous and strictly monotone on \([a,b]\), then \(f^{-1}\) is continuous.
  3. Construct a function that is discontinuous at every point of \([0,1]\).

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
1. Prove that a continuous function on a compact set is uniformly continuous (fill in the details of Theorem 4.6).
  2. Prove that a monotone function has only jump discontinuities, and at most countably many of them.

Hint: In Exercise 8, associate each interval of jump with a rational number; note the endpoint cases.

docs.title: Chapter 5 · Differentiation
docs.text: Status: Expanded. Core theorems are supplied with proofs or explicitly "deferred". Part of: Rudin System · Chapter 5 · Differentiation Source: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Chapter 5.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Sequences, continuity;
  • Spaces, Limits, and Continuity: limits.

docs.title: 5.1 The Derivative
docs.text:
\(f:(a,b)\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at \(x\) if

\[ f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \]

exists.

docs.title: Theorem 5.1 (Differentiable ⇒ Continuous)
docs.text:
If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(f\) is continuous at \(x\).

Proof:

\[ f(x+h)-f(x)=\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\cdot h\to f'(x)\cdot0=0. \]

This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 5.2 (Rules of Differentiation)
docs.text:
If \(f,g\) are differentiable, then

\[ (f+g)'=f'+g',\qquad (fg)'=f'g+fg',\qquad \left(\frac fg\right)'=\frac{f'g-fg'}{g^2}\ (g\ne0). \]

Proof: The first two identities follow directly from the definition of the limit; for the quotient rule, regard \(1/g\) as a composition, or combine the difference quotients over a common denominator. This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 5.3 (Chain Rule)
docs.text:
If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) and \(g\) is differentiable at \(f(x)\), then

\[ (g\circ f)'(x)=g'(f(x))f'(x). \]

Proof sketch: Write

\[ \frac{g(f(x+h))-g(f(x))}{h} =\frac{g(f(x+h))-g(f(x))}{f(x+h)-f(x)}\cdot\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}, \]

and pass to the limit when \(f(x+h)\ne f(x)\); if \(f(x+h)=f(x)\), this case must be treated separately, or the definition may be completed by continuity.

docs.title: Theorem 5.4 (Rolle)
docs.text:
If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and \(f(a)=f(b)\), then there exists \(\xi\in(a,b)\) such that \(f'(\xi)=0\).

Proof: \(f\) attains a maximum and a minimum on the compact interval. If an extremum is attained in the interior, Fermat's lemma yields a vanishing derivative; if both endpoints are extrema, then \(f\) is constant and any \(\xi\) will do. This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 5.5 (Lagrange Mean Value Theorem)
docs.text:
If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), then there exists \(\xi\in(a,b)\) such that

\[ f(b)-f(a)=f'(\xi)(b-a). \]

Proof: Let

\[ g(x)=f(x)-\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(x-a). \]

Then \(g(a)=g(b)\), and Rolle's theorem applies to \(g\). This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 5.6 (Cauchy Mean Value Theorem)
docs.text:
If \(f,g\) are continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), with \(g'(x)\ne0\), then there exists \(\xi\) such that

\[ \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{g(b)-g(a)}=\frac{f'(\xi)}{g'(\xi)}. \]

Proof: Apply Rolle's theorem to

\[ h(x)=f(x)(g(b)-g(a))-g(x)(f(b)-f(a)). \]

This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 5.7 (Darboux Property of the Derivative)
docs.text:
The derivative possesses the intermediate value property: if \(f\) is differentiable on an interval, then \(f'\) assumes every value between any two of its values.

Proof sketch: Let \(a<b\) and \(f'(a)<\lambda<f'(b)\). Consider \(g(x)=f(x)-\lambda x\); near the endpoints the monotonicity of \(g\) is of opposite character, hence \(g\) attains an extremum in the interior, and Fermat's lemma gives \(g'=0\), that is, \(f'=\lambda\).

docs.title: Theorem 5.8 (Taylor's Theorem, Lagrange Remainder)
docs.text:
If \(f\) has \(n\) derivatives on an interval containing \(a\), then

\[ f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k +\frac{f^{(n)}(\xi)}{n!}(x-a)^n \]

holds for some \(\xi\) between \(a\) and \(x\).

Proof sketch: Denote the remainder by \(R_n(x)\), construct an auxiliary function and apply Rolle's theorem repeatedly; or apply the MVT for \(n=1\) and then proceed by induction.

docs.title: Theorem 5.9 (L'Hôpital's Rule)
docs.text:
In the \(0/0\) or \(\infty/\infty\) case, if \(\lim f'/g'=L\), then \(\lim f/g=L\) (under suitable neighbourhood and differentiability conditions).

Proof status: The full proof is deferred; the essential ingredients are the Cauchy Mean Value Theorem and the treatment of endpoint limits. Before use, the type of the indeterminate form and the neighbourhood conditions must be verified.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
1. Determine the intervals of monotonicity and the extrema of \(f(x)=x^3-3x\).
  2. Use the MVT to prove: if \(f'\equiv0\), then \(f\) is constant.
  3. Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x-x}{x^3}\).

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
1. Prove that \(e^x\ge1+x\) for all \(x\).
  2. Prove: if \(f'\) is bounded, then \(f\) is uniformly continuous.
  3. Use Taylor's formula to estimate the error of the third-order approximation of \(\sin x\) near \(0\).

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
1. Prove the Darboux property of the derivative.
  2. Construct a differentiable function whose derivative is discontinuous, and explain why the Darboux property nevertheless holds.

Hint: for Exercise 8, consider \(x^2\sin(1/x)\) (\(x\ne0\)) together with \(f(0)=0\).
