docs.title: Chapter 6 · The Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
docs.text: Status: Expanded. Key steps are supplied for existence proofs; major theorems are explicitly marked. Part of: Rudin System · Chapter 6 · The Riemann–Stieltjes Integral Source: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Chapter 6.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Sequences, continuity, differentiation;
  • Chapter 2: compactness and uniform continuity;
  • Spaces, Limits, and Continuity: metric spaces.

docs.title: 6.1 Partitions and Upper and Lower Sums
docs.text:
Let \([a,b]\) be an interval and let \(f,\alpha:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) be bounded. A partition is

\[ P=\{a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b\}. \]

Let

\[ M_i=\sup_{[x_{i-1},x_i]}f,\qquad m_i=\inf_{[x_{i-1},x_i]}f, \]

and define the upper and lower sums:

\[ U(P,f,\alpha)=\sum_{i=1}^n M_i\Delta\alpha_i, \qquad L(P,f,\alpha)=\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\Delta\alpha_i, \]

where \(\Delta\alpha_i=\alpha(x_i)-\alpha(x_{i-1})\) (we first assume that \(\alpha\) is monotonically increasing, so that these are nonnegative).

Define

\[ \overline{\int_a^b}f\,d\alpha=\inf_P U(P,f,\alpha), \qquad \underline{\int_a^b}f\,d\alpha=\sup_P L(P,f,\alpha). \]

If the upper and lower integrals coincide, we say that the Riemann–Stieltjes integral exists and write it as \(\int_a^b f\,d\alpha\).

docs.title: Theorem 6.1 (Refinement of a Partition)
docs.text:
If \(P^*\) is a refinement of \(P\), then

\[ L(P,f,\alpha)\le L(P^*,f,\alpha)\le U(P^*,f,\alpha)\le U(P,f,\alpha). \]

Proof idea: It suffices to consider the insertion of a single division point into one subinterval; the supremum over a smaller interval does not exceed the original supremum, and the infimum behaves in the opposite way. Adding the resulting inequalities term by term yields the claim.

docs.title: Theorem 6.2 (Necessary and Sufficient Condition for Integrability)
docs.text:
\(f\) is integrable with respect to \(\alpha\) \(\iff\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a partition \(P\) such that

\[ U(P,f,\alpha)-L(P,f,\alpha)<\varepsilon. \]

Proof outline:

  • If \(f\) is integrable, choose \(P_1,P_2\) so that the upper and lower sums are close to the upper and lower integrals, and squeeze by means of a common refinement;
  • Conversely, the upper and lower integrals are trapped between two numbers whose difference is less than \(\varepsilon\); letting \(\varepsilon\to0\) shows that they are equal.

docs.title: Theorem 6.3 (Continuous × Monotone)
docs.text:
If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(\alpha\) is monotonically increasing on \([a,b]\), then \(\int_a^b f\,d\alpha\) exists.

Proof: \(f\) is uniformly continuous on the compact interval. Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-y|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon\). Take a partition \(P\) all of whose subintervals have length \(<\delta\). Then

\[ M_i-m_i<\varepsilon, \]

so that

\[ U(P,f,\alpha)-L(P,f,\alpha) \le \varepsilon\sum_{i=1}^n\Delta\alpha_i =\varepsilon(\alpha(b)-\alpha(a)). \]

Integrability follows from Theorem 6.2. This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 6.4 (Bounded Variation × Continuous)
docs.text:
If \(\alpha\) is of bounded variation on \([a,b]\) and \(f\) is continuous, then \(\int f\,d\alpha\) exists.

Proof status: The full proof is deferred. Idea: write \(\alpha\) as the difference of two monotonically increasing functions, \(\alpha=\alpha_1-\alpha_2\) (Jordan decomposition), apply Theorem 6.3 to \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) separately, and then subtract.

docs.title: 6.3 Properties of the Integral
docs.text:
If \(f,g\) are integrable with respect to \(\alpha\), then:

[ \int(\lambda f+\mu g)\,d\alpha=\lambda\int f\,d\alpha+\mu\int g\,d\alpha, ] [ \int f\,d(\lambda\alpha+\mu\beta)=\lambda\int f\,d\alpha+\mu\int f\,d\beta, ] [ \left|\int f\,d\alpha\right|\le\int|f|\,d\alpha\quad(\alpha\text{ monotonically increasing}). ]

Proof: By the linearity of upper and lower sums together with a squeezing argument; the absolute-value estimate uses \(-|f|\le f\le|f|\). This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 6.5 (Integration by Parts)
docs.text:
If \(f\) is integrable with respect to \(\alpha\), then \(\alpha\) is integrable with respect to \(f\), and

\[ \int_a^b f\,d\alpha+\int_a^b \alpha\,df =f(b)\alpha(b)-f(a)\alpha(a). \]

Proof outline: For a partition \(P\), consider

\[ \sum f(x_i)(\alpha(x_i)-\alpha(x_{i-1})) +\sum \alpha(x_{i-1})(f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})) =f(b)\alpha(b)-f(a)\alpha(a), \]

and pass to the limit.

docs.title: Theorem 6.6 (Change of Variable)
docs.text:
If \(\varphi:[\alpha,\beta]\to[a,b]\) is continuously differentiable and strictly monotone, and \(f\) is continuous, then

\[ \int_{\varphi(\alpha)}^{\varphi(\beta)}f(x)\,dx =\int_\alpha^\beta f(\varphi(t))\varphi'(t)\,dt. \]

Proof status: The full proof is deferred; it uses the Lagrange mean value theorem applied to Riemann sums together with uniform continuity.

docs.title: 6.4 Rectifiable Curves
docs.text:
The arc length of a curve \(\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n\) is

\[ L(\gamma)=\sup_{P}\sum_{i=1}^n\|\gamma(x_i)-\gamma(x_{i-1})\|. \]

If \(L(\gamma)<\infty\), we say that \(\gamma\) is rectifiable.

docs.title: Theorem 6.7 (Rectifiable ↔ Bounded Variation)
docs.text:
\(\gamma\) is rectifiable \(\iff\) each coordinate function \(\gamma_j\) is of bounded variation on \([a,b]\).

Proof outline: Use the equivalence of norms and the definition of bounded variation, estimating coordinate by coordinate; all norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
1. For \(f(x)=x\) and \([a,b]=[0,1]\), compute \(\int_0^1 x\,dx\) directly from the definition.
  2. Prove: if \(f\) is bounded on \([a,b]\) and \(\alpha\) is monotonically increasing, then \(L(P,f,\alpha)\le U(P,f,\alpha)\).
  3. Compute \(\int_0^1 x\,d(x^2)\) (hint: integration by parts).

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
1. Prove that a continuous function is integrable with respect to a monotonically increasing function (completing Theorem 6.3).
  2. Prove the additivity of the integral over intervals: if \(a<c<b\), then \(\int_a^b f\,d\alpha=\int_a^c f\,d\alpha+\int_c^b f\,d\alpha\).
  3. Prove: if \(f\) is continuous and \(\alpha\) is of bounded variation, then \(|\int f\,d\alpha|\le\|f\|_\infty V(\alpha)\).

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
1. Prove the integration by parts formula (completing the limiting step of Theorem 6.5).
  2. Prove that the arc length of a \(C^1\) curve equals \(\int_a^b\|\gamma'(t)\|\,dt\).

Hint: For Exercise 8, first apply the MVT to a partition to obtain a lower bound, and then use uniform continuity to obtain an upper bound.

docs.title: Chapter 7 · Sequences of Functions and Series of Functions
docs.text: Status: Expanded. Proofs are supplied for the core theorems on uniform convergence; Arzelà–Ascoli and Stone–Weierstrass are stated with their guiding ideas. Part of: Rudin System · Chapter 7 · Sequences of Functions and Series of Functions Source: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Chapter 7.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Continuity, differentiation, integration;
  • Chapter 3: series;
  • Chapter 2: compactness.

docs.title: 7.1 Pointwise and Uniform Convergence
docs.text:
A sequence of functions \(f_n:X\to Y\) converges pointwise to \(f\) if for every \(x\), \(f_n(x)\to f(x)\). Uniform convergence: if

\[ \forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists N,\ \forall n>N,\ \forall x\in X:\ d_Y(f_n(x),f(x))<\varepsilon. \]

Equivalently, \(\sup_{x\in X}d_Y(f_n(x),f(x))\to0\).

docs.title: Theorem 7.1 (Uniform convergence ⇒ pointwise convergence)
docs.text:
Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence.

Proof: Immediate from the definition. Q.E.D.

docs.title: Theorem 7.2 (Uniform convergence preserves continuity)
docs.text:
If \(f_n\) is continuous and \(f_n\rightrightarrows f\) converges uniformly, then \(f\) is continuous.

Proof: Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(N\) such that \(d(f_n(x),f(x))<\varepsilon/3\) for all \(x\) whenever \(n>N\). Fix \(n>N\); since \(f_n\) is continuous, choose \(\delta>0\) such that \(d(x,y)<\delta\Rightarrow d(f_n(x),f_n(y))<\varepsilon/3\). Then

\[ d(f(x),f(y))\le d(f(x),f_n(x))+d(f_n(x),f_n(y))+d(f_n(y),f(y))<\varepsilon. \]

Q.E.D.

docs.title: Theorem 7.3 (Interchange of uniform convergence and integration)
docs.text:
If \(f_n\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(f_n\rightrightarrows f\), then

\[ \int_a^b f_n\to\int_a^b f. \]

Proof:

\[ \left|\int f_n-\int f\right|\le\int|f_n-f|\le(b-a)\|f_n-f\|_\infty\to0. \]

Q.E.D.

docs.title: Theorem 7.4 (Interchange of uniform convergence and differentiation)
docs.text:
If \(f_n\) is differentiable on \([a,b]\), \(f_n(x_0)\) converges, and \(f_n'\) converges uniformly to \(g\) on \([a,b]\), then \(f_n\) converges uniformly to some \(f\), and \(f'=g\).

Proof sketch: Use the MVT on \(f_n-f_m\) to control the difference and first establish uniform convergence; then pass to the limit in

\[ f_n(x)=f_n(x_0)+\int_{x_0}^x f_n'(t)\,dt \]

and apply Theorem 7.3 to obtain \(f(x)=f(x_0)+\int g\), so that \(f'=g\).

docs.title: 7.2 Series of Functions
docs.text: If the partial sums of \(\sum f_n\) converge uniformly, the series is said to converge uniformly.

docs.title: Theorem 7.5 (Weierstrass M-test)
docs.text:
If \(|f_n(x)|\le M_n\) and \(\sum M_n<\infty\), then \(\sum f_n\) converges uniformly.

Proof: By the Cauchy criterion, for \(m>n\),

\[ \left|\sum_{k=n+1}^m f_k(x)\right|\le\sum_{k=n+1}^m M_k\to0, \]

independently of \(x\), hence the series is uniformly Cauchy. Q.E.D.

docs.title: 7.3 Equicontinuity and Arzelà–Ascoli
docs.text: A family of functions \(\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Y)\) is equicontinuous if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(d(f(x),f(y))<\varepsilon\) for all \(f\in\mathcal F\) whenever \(d(x,y)<\delta\).

docs.title: Theorem 7.6 (Arzelà–Ascoli)
docs.text:
If \(X\) is compact and \(\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,\mathbb R^n)\) is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous, then \(\mathcal F\) contains a subsequence that converges in the uniform metric.

Proof status: Full proof deferred. Idea: take a countable dense subset of \(X\) and use the diagonal argument to extract a pointwise convergent subsequence; equicontinuity then upgrades pointwise convergence to uniform convergence.

docs.title: Theorem 7.7 (Stone–Weierstrass)
docs.text:
If \(X\) is compact and \(\mathcal A\subseteq C(X,\mathbb R)\) is an algebra of functions containing the constants and separating points (for any \(x\ne y\) there exists \(f\in\mathcal A\) with \(f(x)\ne f(y)\)), then \(\mathcal A\) is uniformly dense in \(C(X,\mathbb R)\).

Proof status: Full proof deferred. The classical proof uses the Weierstrass approximation theorem together with lattice methods.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
1. Determine whether \(f_n(x)=x^n\) converges uniformly on \([0,1]\).
  2. Determine whether \(f_n(x)=x/n\) converges uniformly on \(\mathbb R\).
  3. Use the M-test to prove that \(\sum x^n/n!\) converges uniformly on every bounded interval.

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
1. Prove that uniform convergence preserves continuity (complete Theorem 7.2).
  2. Construct a sequence of continuous functions converging pointwise to a discontinuous function, showing that pointwise convergence does not suffice.
  3. Prove that if \(f_n\) converges uniformly and each \(f_n\) is bounded, then the limit is bounded.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
1. Prove the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem (one may first prove the case \(X=[0,1]\)).
  2. Use Stone–Weierstrass to prove that the polynomials are uniformly dense in \(C[0,1]\).

Hint: for Exercise 8, take \(\mathcal A\) to be the algebra of polynomials, verify that it contains the constants and separates points, and then invoke the theorem.

docs.title: Chapter 8 · Special Functions
docs.text: Status: Expanded. The focus is to bring the exponential function, the logarithm, the trigonometric functions, Fourier series, and the Gamma function into a unified framework. Part of: Rudin System · Chapter 8 · Special Functions Source: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Chapter 8.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 3: Power series;
  • Chapter 5: Differentiation;
  • Chapters 6–7: Integration, uniform convergence.

docs.title: 8.1 The Exponential Function
docs.text:
Definition

\[ e^z=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{z^n}{n!},\qquad z\in\mathbb C. \]

The series converges absolutely on the whole plane (ratio test), and converges uniformly on every compact set.

docs.title: Theorem 8.1 (Law of Exponents)
docs.text:
\[ e^{z+w}=e^z e^w. \]

Proof: By the Cauchy product of absolutely convergent series,

\[ e^z e^w=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{z^k}{k!}\frac{w^{n-k}}{(n-k)!} =\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(z+w)^n}{n!}=e^{z+w}. \]

This completes the proof.

Corollary: \(e^0=1\), \(e^{-z}=1/e^z\), \(e^z\ne0\).

docs.title: Theorem 8.2 (Derivative)
docs.text:
\[ (e^z)'=e^z. \]

Proof: Differentiate term by term (a power series converges uniformly on compact sets),

\[ \frac{d}{dz}\sum\frac{z^n}{n!}=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{z^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}=e^z. \]

This completes the proof.

docs.title: 8.2 The Logarithmic Function
docs.text:
For \(x>0\), define

\[ \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}. \]

docs.title: Theorem 8.3 (Properties of the Logarithm)
docs.text:
\[ \log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(e^x)=x,\qquad e^{\log x}=x. \]

Proof: The substitution \(t=xu\) gives

\[ \log(xy)=\int_1^{xy}\frac{dt}{t} =\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}+\int_x^{xy}\frac{dt}{t} =\log x+\int_1^y\frac{du}{u}=\log x+\log y. \]

The remaining two identities follow from the definition and the inverse function theorem. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 8.3 The Trigonometric Functions
docs.text:
Definition

\[ \cos z=\frac{e^{iz}+e^{-iz}}2,\qquad \sin z=\frac{e^{iz}-e^{-iz}}{2i}. \]

Then

[ \cos^2 z+\sin^2 z=1,\qquad \sin(z+w)=\sin z\cos w+\cos z\sin w, ] [ (\sin z)'=\cos z,\qquad (\cos z)'=-\sin z. ]

\(\pi\) is defined as \(2\) times the smallest positive zero; the periodicity of the trigonometric functions follows from this.

docs.title: 8.4 Fourier Series
docs.text:
Let \(f\) be \(2\pi\)-periodic and Riemann integrable on \([-\pi,\pi]\). The Fourier coefficients are:

\[ \hat f(n)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(t)e^{-int}\,dt, \]

The Fourier series is:

\[ f(x)\sim\sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty\hat f(n)e^{inx}. \]

docs.title: Theorem 8.4 (Fourier Convergence, Overview)
docs.text:
If \(f\) is piecewise \(C^1\) on \([-\pi,\pi]\), then the Fourier series converges at every point to

\[ \frac{f(x+)+f(x-)}2. \]

In particular, at points of continuity it converges to \(f(x)\).

Proof status: The full proof is deferred; it requires the Dirichlet kernel and the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma.

docs.title: Theorem 8.5 (Parseval)
docs.text:
If \(f\in L^2[-\pi,\pi]\), then

\[ \frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|f(x)|^2\,dx =\sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty|\hat f(n)|^2. \]

Proof status: Deferred; it requires the completeness of \(L^2\) and a Fourier basis.

docs.title: 8.5 The Gamma Function
docs.text:
For \(x>0\), define

\[ \Gamma(x)=\int_0^\infty t^{x-1}e^{-t}\,dt. \]

docs.title: Theorem 8.6 (Recurrence and Analytic Continuation)
docs.text:
\[ \Gamma(x+1)=x\Gamma(x),\qquad \Gamma(n+1)=n!. \]

\(\Gamma\) admits an analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on \(\mathbb C\setminus\{0,-1,-2,\dots\}\), with a simple pole at \(x=-n\) and residue \((-1)^n/n!\).

Proof: Integration by parts yields the recurrence; the continuation is obtained from \(\Gamma(x)\Gamma(1-x)=\pi/\sin(\pi x)\) or the Weierstrass product. This completes the proof.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
1. Prove that \(e^z\ne0\) for all \(z\in\mathbb C\).
  2. Find an integral representation of \(\log 2\) and show that its value lies between \(1/2\) and \(1\).
  3. Prove that \(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1\).

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
1. Prove that \(e^x>1+x\) for \(x>0\).
  2. Compute the Fourier coefficients of \(f(x)=x\) on \([-\pi,\pi]\).
  3. Prove that \(\Gamma(1)=1\) and \(\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi\).

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
1. Prove that Parseval's identity holds for trigonometric polynomials, and explain how to approximate a general \(L^2\) function.
  2. Use Fourier series to prove that \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty 1/n^2=\pi^2/6\) (hint: expand \(f(x)=x^2\)).

docs.title: Chapter 9 · Multivariable Functions
docs.text: Status: Expanded. The inverse and implicit function theorems are given with their conditions and the idea of the proof; the complete proofs are marked as deferred. Belongs to: Rudin System · Chapter 9 · Multivariable Functions Source: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Chapter 9.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Linear algebra;
  • Spaces, Limits, and Continuity: metric spaces, compactness;
  • Chapters 4–5: continuity, differentiation.

docs.title: 9.1 Linear Transformations and Norms
docs.text:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Define the operator norm

\[ \|A\|=\sup_{\|x\|=1}\|Ax\|. \]

Then \(\|Ax\|\le\|A\|\|x\|\), and

\[ \|A+B\|\le\|A\|+\|B\|,\qquad \|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|. \]

docs.title: Theorem 9.1 (Continuity of Finite-Dimensional Linear Transformations)
docs.text:
Every linear map \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuous.

Proof: Let the matrix entries of \(A\) be \(a_{ij}\). Then

\[ \|Ax-Ay\|=\|A(x-y)\|\le\|A\|\|x-y\|, \]

so take \(\delta=\varepsilon/\|A\|\) (the case \(\|A\|=0\) is trivial). This completes the proof.

docs.title: 9.2 Derivatives
docs.text:
We say that \(f:\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is differentiable at \(x\) if there exists a linear map \(Df(x):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) such that

\[ f(x+h)-f(x)=Df(x)h+o(\|h\|). \]

\(Df(x)\) is the Jacobian matrix.

docs.title: Theorem 9.2 (Differentiable ⇒ Continuous)
docs.text:
Differentiability implies continuity.

Proof:

\[ \|f(x+h)-f(x)\|\le\|Df(x)\|\|h\|+o(\|h\|)\to0. \]

This completes the proof.

docs.title: Theorem 9.3 (Chain Rule)
docs.text:
If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) and \(g\) is differentiable at \(f(x)\), then

\[ D(g\circ f)(x)=Dg(f(x))\,Df(x). \]

Proof sketch: Expand \(g(f(x+h))-g(f(x))\) as \(Dg(f(x))(f(x+h)-f(x))+o(\|f(x+h)-f(x)\|)\), then use the differentiability of \(f\).

docs.title: 9.3 Contraction Mappings and the Inverse Function Theorem
Theorem 9.4 (Contraction Mapping Principle)
docs.text:
If \((X,d)\) is complete and \(T:X\to X\) satisfies \(d(Tx,Ty)\le qd(x,y)\) with \(0\le q<1\), then \(T\) has a unique fixed point.

Proof: See proof page §15.

docs.title: Theorem 9.5 (Inverse Function Theorem)
docs.text:
Let \(f:\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be \(C^1\), let \(a\in\Omega\), and suppose \(Df(a)\) is invertible. Then there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(a\) and a neighborhood \(V\) of \(f(a)\) such that \(f:U\to V\) is a \(C^1\) homeomorphism, and

\[ D(f^{-1})(y)=[Df(f^{-1}(y))]^{-1}. \]

Proof sketch: Set \(F(x)=x+[Df(a)]^{-1}(y-f(x))\), thereby converting the equation \(f(x)=y\) into a fixed-point problem for \(F\); near \(a\), use the continuity of \(Df\) together with the contraction mapping principle, and then show that the inverse map is differentiable.

docs.title: Theorem 9.6 (Implicit Function Theorem)
docs.text:
If \(F:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to\mathbb R^m\) is \(C^1\), \(F(a,b)=0\), and \(\partial F/\partial y(a,b)\) is invertible, then there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(a\) and a unique \(C^1\) function \(g:U\to\mathbb R^m\) such that \(g(a)=b\) and

\[ F(x,g(x))=0. \]

Proof sketch: Apply the inverse function theorem to \(G(x,y)=(x,F(x,y))\), and then take the second component of the local inverse.

docs.title: Theorem 9.7 (Rank Theorem, Statement)
docs.text:
If \(f\) is \(C^1\) near \(a\) and \(Df(a)\) has rank \(r\), then there exists a local change of coordinates that reduces \(f\) to

\[ (x_1,\dots,x_n)\mapsto(x_1,\dots,x_r,0,\dots,0). \]

Proof status: Deferred; it requires the inverse function theorem and a linear change of coordinates.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
1. Compute the Jacobian of \(f(x,y)=(x^2y,\sin y)\).
  2. Prove that \(\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|\).
  3. Determine whether \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) is differentiable at \((0,0)\).

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
1. Prove the chain rule (completing the \(o(\|h\|)\) estimate in Theorem 9.3).
  2. Use the contraction mapping principle to prove that the equation \(x=\cos x\) has a unique solution in \([0,1]\).
  3. Explain why the invertibility of \(Df(a)\) is necessary in the inverse function theorem (give a counterexample).

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
1. Prove the implicit function theorem (deriving it from the inverse function theorem).
  2. Prove the linear-algebra case of the rank theorem, and then explain how to extend it by means of the inverse function theorem.

Hint: For Exercise 8, first carry out the rank factorization of the linear map \(A=P\begin{pmatrix}I_r&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}Q\).

docs.title: Chapter 10 · Integration of Differential Forms
docs.text: Status: Expanded. Stokes' theorem is given with a statement and a proof sketch; the complete proof requires the inverse/implicit function tools of Chapter 9. Part of: Rudin System · Chapter 10 · Integration of Differential Forms Source: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Chapter 10.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Linear algebra, determinants;
  • Chapter 9: multivariable differentiation, inverse function theorem;
  • Chapter 6: integration.

docs.title: 10.1 Differential Forms
docs.text:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open. A \(k\)-form can be written as

\[ \omega=\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n} f_{i_1\cdots i_k}(x)\,dx_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_{i_k}, \]

where \(f_I\) are smooth functions and \(\wedge\) is the antisymmetric bilinear product:

\[ dx_i\wedge dx_j=-dx_j\wedge dx_i,\qquad dx_i\wedge dx_i=0. \]

Exterior differentiation:

\[ d\omega=\sum_I df_I\wedge dx_I =\sum_I\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{\partial f_I}{\partial x_j}dx_j\wedge dx_I. \]

docs.title: Theorem 10.1 (d² = 0)
docs.text:
For a smooth form \(\omega\), we have

\[ d(d\omega)=0. \]

Proof: By

\[ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j} =\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_j\partial x_i} \]

and \(dx_i\wedge dx_j=-dx_j\wedge dx_i\), the mixed partial derivative terms cancel in pairs. This completes the proof.

Closed form: \(d\omega=0\). Exact form: \(\omega=d\eta\). Theorem 10.1 shows that exact ⇒ closed; the converse is in general false and depends on the topology of the domain.

docs.title: 10.2 Simplices and Chains
docs.text:
The standard \(k\)-simplex:

\[ \Delta^k=\left\{(t_1,\dots,t_k):t_i\ge0,\ \sum t_i\le1\right\}. \]

A singular \(k\)-simplex is a smooth mapping \(\sigma:\Delta^k\to U\). A \(k\)-chain is a finite formal sum \(\sum a_i\sigma_i\).

Boundary:

\[ \partial\sigma=\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^i\sigma\circ F_i, \]

where \(F_i\) is the affine mapping that embeds the \(i\)-th face of the standard simplex.

docs.title: Theorem 10.2 (∂² = 0)
docs.text:
\[ \partial(\partial\sigma)=0. \]

Proof: One computes term by term according to the composition of face mappings; the signs \((-1)^{i+j}\) cancel when the two face mappings are interchanged. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 10.3 Integration of Forms and Stokes' Theorem
docs.text:
For a \(k\)-form \(\omega\) and a singular \(k\)-simplex \(\sigma\), define

\[ \int_\sigma\omega=\int_{\Delta^k}\sigma^*\omega. \]

This extends linearly to chains.

docs.title: Theorem 10.3 (Stokes)
docs.text:
If \(\omega\) is a smooth \((k-1)\)-form on \(U\) and \(c\) is a \(k\)-chain, then

\[ \int_{\partial c}\omega=\int_c d\omega. \]

Proof sketch: First prove the statement for the standard simplex and monomial forms; use Fubini's theorem to reduce the boundary integral to an iterated integral, then apply the fundamental theorem of calculus; finally extend by pullbacks and the linearity of chains.

Special cases:

  • \(k=1\): \(\int_a^b f'(x)dx=f(b)-f(a)\);
  • \(k=2\): Green's formula;
  • \(k=3\): the classical Stokes and Gauss formulas.

docs.title: Theorem 10.4 (Poincaré Lemma)
docs.text:
If \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a star-shaped region and \(\omega\) is a closed \(k\)-form (\(k\ge1\)), then there exists a \((k-1)\)-form \(\eta\) such that

\[ \omega=d\eta. \]

Proof status: The complete proof is deferred. The construction uses a radial homotopy: integrate \(\omega\) along the line segment from \(x\) to the origin to obtain \(\eta\); closedness guarantees that \(d\eta=\omega\).

Corollary: In \(\mathbb R^n\), every closed form is locally exact; whether it is globally exact is measured by de Rham cohomology.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
1. Compute \(d(x\,dy+y\,dz)\).
  2. Verify that \(d(dx\wedge dy)=0\).
  3. Write out the correspondence between Green's formula and Stokes' theorem in \(\mathbb R^2\).

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
1. Prove that \(d^2=0\) (supply the sign cancellation).
  2. Prove that \(\partial^2=0\) holds in the case \(k=2\).
  3. Determine whether \(\omega=x\,dy-y\,dx\) is exact on \(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}\).

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
1. Prove the Poincaré lemma on a star-shaped region (write out the radial homotopy formula).
  2. Use Stokes' theorem to prove that if \(f\) is holomorphic on the unit disk, then the integral over a closed path is 0 (compare with complex analysis).

Hint: For Exercise 6, compute \(d\omega\) and use the angular form to show that it is not globally exact.

docs.title: 11.1 Measure
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal M\) be a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(X\): it contains \(X\) and is closed under complements and countable unions. A measure \(\mu:\mathcal M\to[0,\infty]\) is a mapping satisfying:

  1. \(\mu(\varnothing)=0\);
  2. nonnegativity;
  3. countable additivity: if the \(A_i\) are pairwise disjoint, then
\[ \mu\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^\infty\mu(A_i). \]

\((X,\mathcal M,\mu)\) is called a measure space. Lebesgue measure is the unique Borel measure on \(\mathbb R^n\) that is translation-invariant and normalized (in the sense of completion).

docs.title: 11.2 Measurable Functions
docs.text:
\(f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]\) is measurable if, for every \(a\in\mathbb R\),

\[ f^{-1}((a,\infty])\in\mathcal M. \]

Equivalently, \(\{f>a\}\) is measurable for every \(a\).

Properties: Sums, products, limits, suprema, and infima of measurable functions are again measurable (under suitable conditions that avoid \(\infty-\infty\)).

docs.title: Theorem 11.1 (Approximation by Simple Functions)
docs.text:
A nonnegative measurable function \(f\) can be written as the pointwise increasing limit of a sequence of simple functions:

\[ f=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi_n,\qquad 0\le\phi_1\le\phi_2\le\cdots \]

Proof outline: Stratify the range in layers of \(2^{-n}\), truncate at \(n\), and construct \(\phi_n\).

docs.title: 11.3 The Lebesgue Integral
docs.text:
For a nonnegative simple function \(\phi=\sum a_i\chi_{A_i}\), define

\[ \int\phi\,d\mu=\sum a_i\mu(A_i). \]

For nonnegative measurable \(f\), define

\[ \int f\,d\mu=\sup\left\{\int\phi\,d\mu:0\le\phi\le f,\ \phi\text{ simple}\right\}. \]

For a general measurable \(f\), write \(f=f^+-f^-\); if \(\int f^+,\int f^-<\infty\), we say that \(f\) is integrable and define

\[ \int f\,d\mu=\int f^+d\mu-\int f^-d\mu. \]

docs.title: Theorem 11.2 (Monotone Convergence Theorem, MCT)
docs.text:
If \(0\le f_n\uparrow f\) and the \(f_n\) are measurable, then

\[ \int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu. \]

Proof status: The full proof is deferred; use approximation by simple functions together with the interchange of suprema.

docs.title: Theorem 11.3 (Fatou's Lemma)
docs.text:
If \(f_n\ge0\) is measurable, then

\[ \int\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu \le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu. \]

Proof: Apply MCT to \(g_n=\inf_{k\ge n}f_k\), and then compare with \(g_n\le f_n\).

docs.title: Theorem 11.4 (Dominated Convergence Theorem, DCT)
docs.text:
If the \(f_n\) are measurable, \(f_n\to f\) a.e., and there exists an integrable \(g\) such that \(|f_n|\le g\) a.e., then

\[ \int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu. \]

Proof: Apply Fatou's lemma to \(g+f_n\ge0\) and to \(g-f_n\ge0\) separately, and squeeze out the conclusion. This completes the proof.

docs.title: 11.4 Relation to the Riemann Integral
docs.text: If \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a,b]\), then \(f\) is Lebesgue integrable, and the two integrals have the same value. The converse fails: the Dirichlet function \(\mathbf 1_{\mathbb Q}\) is not Riemann integrable, but its Lebesgue integral is 0 (because \(\mathbb Q\) has measure zero).

docs.title: Theorem 11.5 (Lebesgue Characterization of Riemann Integrability)
docs.text:
A bounded \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Riemann integrable \(\iff\) the set of discontinuities of \(f\) is a set of Lebesgue measure zero.

Proof status: The full proof is deferred; use the oscillation function and the definition of a set of measure zero.

docs.title: 11.5 L² Spaces
docs.text:
\[ L^2(\mu)=\left\{f:\int|f|^2\,d\mu<\infty\right\}, \]

equipped with the inner product

\[ \langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g\,d\mu. \]

docs.title: Theorem 11.6 (Riesz–Fischer)
docs.text:
\(L^2(\mu)\) is a complete inner product space (a Hilbert space).

Proof status: Deferred; take a subsequence of a Cauchy sequence that converges a.e., and then control it by means of Fatou's lemma.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
1. Prove that every countable set is a set of Lebesgue measure zero.
  2. Determine whether \(\mathbf 1_{\mathbb Q}\) is Riemann integrable and whether it is Lebesgue integrable on \([0,1]\).
  3. Use MCT to compute \(\int_0^1\sum_{n\ge1}x^n\,dx\).

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
1. Prove Fatou's lemma (from MCT).
  2. Prove DCT (from Fatou's lemma).
  3. Give an example showing that the hypothesis "the dominating function \(g\) is integrable" cannot be removed from DCT.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
1. Prove the Riesz–Fischer theorem (one may first prove that every \(L^2\) Cauchy sequence has a subsequence that converges a.e.).
  2. Prove: a bounded function is Riemann integrable if and only if its set of discontinuities is a set of measure zero.

Hint: For Exercise 8, use the oscillation \(\omega(x)\) and the set \(\{x:\omega(x)\ge1/k\}\).
